Changes in tumour microenvironment composition strongly influence this polarisation and drive adaptive transcriptional responses more profoundly than chemoradiation alone. Mechanistically, JBS genes are enriched for promoters marked by persistent bivalent chromatin and neurodevelopmental regulatory programmes. These findings suggest that JARID2-associated Polycomb regulation maintains a reservoir of developmental plasticity that enables treatment-driven ecosystem adaptation and represents a potential therapeutic vulnerability.

items.title: Eukaryotic 45S ribosomal RNA spacers encode an ancient layer of antiviral response
items.corresponding_institution: Edward Via College of Osteopathic Medicine
items.abstract: Eukaryotic 45S ribosomal RNA genes produce internal transcribed spacers (ITSs) that are excised and discarded during ribosome biogenesis, with no established function beyond rRNA processing. Here, we uncover an unexpected antiviral role for these seemingly expendable sequences. Comparative genomic analyses reveal extensive, evolutionarily widespread sequence similarities between eukaryotic ITSs and DNA viruses, particularly between vertebrate ITSs and herpesviruses. Across herpesvirus infections, ITS transcripts undergo striking, virus-specific remodeling, largely uncoupled from mature ribosomal RNA production. During herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) infection, hierarchical Bayesian comparison of competing dynamical models favors active host ITS deployment over passive viral remodeling by odds of 174,000:1. Experimental depletion of ITS2 consistently increases infectious HSV-1 production by approximately 70%, whereas supplementation with synthetic ITS2 RNA generally suppresses viral replication. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized antiviral activity within the 45S rRNA system, challenging the view of ITSs as disposable byproducts of ribosome biogenesis.

items.title: Local and network-level dynamics of alpha and beta rhythms during visuospatial attention in autism
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Psychosomatic Medicine and Psychotherapy, University Hospital Frankfurt, Goethe-University Frankfurt
items.abstract: Visuospatial attention is altered in autism, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Neural oscillatory activity coordinates distributed processes supporting attentional selection and their flexible adjustment to changing environmental demands. Altered oscillatory organization may therefore provide a mechanistic basis for atypical attentional processing in autism. We tested this theory using EEG recordings from 80 autistic and neurotypical children and youth performing a spatial cueing task with valid and invalid cues. We quantified alpha- and beta-band measures of local power and inter-trial phase clustering (ITPC) together with power- and phase-based measures of posterior-frontal long-range connectivity. Across validity conditions, autistic participants showed a more frontal alpha distribution, reduced posterior alpha lateralization and posterior beta ITPC, and higher frontal beta power. Crucially, autistic participants also presented reduced neural adaptation across attentional conditions, reflected in attenuated validity-dependent modulation of alpha power and of posterior-frontal beta connectivity, with elevated beta connectivity particularly in the valid cue condition. This neural pattern was accompanied by greater reaction-time slowing in the invalid compared with the valid cue condition. Within autistic participants, beta dynamics showed nominal associations with restricted and repetitive behaviors that did not survive multiple-comparison correction. Together, these findings suggest that visuospatial attention in autism is characterized by altered local oscillatory organization, combined with reduced modulation of local and distributed dynamics as attentional demands change. Alterations in alpha and beta activity may reflect reduced spatially selective attentional gating alongside greater maintenance of established attentional states.

items.title: Music and speech dissociate local temporal irregularity from response strength in human superior temporal cortex
items.corresponding_institution: University of Science and Technology of China
items.abstract: Speech and music engage overlapping auditory cortex. We asked whether they shape the timing of local activity in ways that regional response strength alone leaves unresolved. In intracranial recordings from 30 participants watching a film with alternating music and speech, 1-10-Hz activity in the superior temporal gyrus (STG) had higher sample entropy during music, indicating that similar short patterns were less likely to persist (mean paired difference = 0.02256, FDR q = 0.00753). The contrast persisted in comparisons of adjacent film blocks and was larger relative to surrogate signals matched for amplitude distribution and approximate power spectrum. Speech elicited higher STG high-frequency power in the intracranial subset and stronger bilateral STG BOLD responses in all 30 participants in the separately acquired fMRI recordings. Together, these findings show that the soundtrack category associated with stronger regional responses differs from the one associated with greater local temporal irregularity. The temporal organisation of local activity therefore adds a dimension to how shared auditory cortex responds to natural sounds.

items.title: Shox2 maintains thalamocortical neuron firing for whisker-based somatomotor responses and sleep spindles in mice
items.corresponding_institution: Neuroscience Program, Brain Institute, Tulane University; Cell and Molecular Biology, Tulane University
items.abstract: In the mouse thalamus, thalamocortical neurons (TCNs) relay sensory information to cortex and generate rhythmic activity, including sleep spindles, through precisely timed firing. TCNs switch between tonic and burst firing modes that depend on intrinsic membrane properties, yet what maintains these properties in the mature thalamus remains unknown. Transcription factors, which regulate the ion channel genes that shape firing, are natural candidates. Here, we investigate Shox2, a transcription factor implicated in rhythmic activity across multiple systems, in ventral posterior medial (VPM) thalamus. Using genetic labeling and optogenetic activation, we show that Shox2 expressing neurons form functional thalamocortical and thalamoreticular projections capable of driving cortical responses. Conditional knockout of Shox2 in VPM alters intrinsic membrane properties, reducing both tonic and burst firing without altering thalamocortical circuit organization or barrel field architecture. These firing deficits are accompanied by impaired whisker-dependent somatomotor performance and a reduction in sleep spindle density in cortical target regions, while overall sleep architecture remains intact. Together, these findings identify Shox2 as a transcriptional regulator required to maintain intrinsic firing modes in VPM thalamocortical neurons, linking a transcription factor to spindle deficits, an emerging neurophysiological biomarker for autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia.

items.title: Neonatal exposure to SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in mice is associated with localized changes in cerebral cortex cell proliferation
items.corresponding_institution: 1. Institute of Biomedical Sciences, Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, 21941902, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
items.abstract: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) can cause acute and persistent neurological manifestations, and evidence suggests these effects may be at least partly explained by direct effects of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) spike protein, which includes neuroinflammation, cognitive dysfunction, and persistent pain. Because the developing brain undergoes finely regulated processes of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and cerebrovascular maturation, exposure to SARS-CoV-2 or its components during this critical period may interfere with neurodevelopment. We therefore investigated whether neonatal exposure to the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein affects processes underlying brain development. To this end, we used a mouse model previously developed by our group, where Swiss mice received an injection (s.c.) of spike protein from the ancestral viral strain or vehicle at postnatal day 1 (P1). Body weight, body length, and the righting reflex were evaluated until postnatal day 20 (P20). At P10, mouse brains were analyzed for cell proliferation, neural cell populations, and cerebrovascular organization, while blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability was assessed at P20 using Evans Blue. Neonatal spike protein exposure did not affect body weight, body length, or postural righting reflex. At P10, cell proliferation in spike-exposed animals was comparable to control groups, whereas region-specific alterations in SOX2-positive cells and TBR1-positive neurons were observed. Spike protein exposure did not broadly alter cerebrovascular architecture or BBB permeability, although increased IB4 fluorescence was detected in the lateral dentate gyrus (DG). Our findings provide evidence that exposure to the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein during postnatal development can influence specific aspects of neural development, highlighting the importance of understanding how viral components may affect the developing brain during critical windows of vulnerability. Keywords: spike protein, brain development, coronavirus, COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2, cerebrovasculature.

items.title: Evolutionarily conserved coupling of lysosomal response sensing and disease-associated microglial reprogramming scales with pathological timescales
items.abstract: Background Microglia transition into disease-associated microglia (DAM) during central nervous system (CNS) injury and neurodegeneration, yet the upstream intracellular logic driving this state conversion in vivo remains unclear. The lysosome acts as a signaling hub, but whether physiological phagocytic load universally initiates and quantitatively couples to DAM reprogramming across different pathological timescales is unknown. Methods We established a rigorous, unit-corrected analytical framework to overcome pseudo-replication in public single-cell data, anchoring statistical inferences at the level of independent biological units (animals, sequencing plates, or donors). We integrated six transcriptomic datasets spanning three murine injury/amyloidosis models and three large-scale human neurodegenerative cohorts (>320,000 microglial nuclei), alongside human Alzheimer's disease (AD) GWAS summary statistics. Results We demonstrate that the MiT/TFE-regulated lysosomal biogenesis program temporally precedes DAM reprogramming and maintains an evolutionarily conserved baseline coupling even in uninjured homeostatic tissue. In human microglia, MITF and TFE3 transcripts closely track DAM activation, whereas post-translationally regulated TFEB mRNA does not. Genetic enrichment analysis (MAGMA) reveals that common AD risk does not act upon the upstream lysosomal program, but is strongly anchored downstream at APOE. Furthermore, Trem2-knockout models demonstrate that disease-induced coupling amplification retains roughly half its magnitude even when the mature DAM subpopulation collapses. Cross-system comparisons reveal a state-transition synchrony model: disease-driven amplification of lysosomal-DAM coupling ({Delta}) scales with pathological timescales, showing strong amplification in acute murine injury and aggressive amyloidosis (5xFAD {Delta} = +0.252), but manifesting primarily as steady baseline maintenance across decades-long asynchronous human AD progression (SEA-AD {Delta} = +0.072). Conclusions Our study establishes the lysosomal stress-DAM coupling as an evolutionarily conserved pacemaking module for microglial state transitions, providing a quantitative framework for therapeutically targeting neuroinflammation and tissue repair.

items.title: Universal barcoded connectomics for massively parallel single-neuron projection mapping in diverse vertebrate species
items.abstract: Neuroscience relies on diverse model species to understand animal behavior and brain function. Yet, tools for rapid, high-resolution brain connectivity mapping remain unavailable in most vertebrate species, slowing progress in many neuroscience models and rendering cross-species circuit comparisons challenging. Here, we overcome this barrier by establishing sequencing-based barcoded connectomics for rapid single-neuron tracing in seven vertebrate species ranging from frogs to birds to non-human primates. We develop a general solution to viral tropism and barcode trafficking, validate our reagents by mapping the projections of thousands of neurons in the songbird HVC, and discover a single set of reagents that functions across highly divergent species. Together, we provide ready-to-use barcoding reagents for diverse species and a simple framework for further adapting them if necessary, enabling high throughput single-neuron tracing across vertebrates.

items.title: Identification of SAMD4B as a Centrosome-Associated Regulator of the Sonic Hedgehog Signaling Pathway
items.abstract: Background: Many protein-protein interactions are required for the assembly and function of primary cilia, microtubule-based organelles critical for the Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling pathway and, in turn, for embryonic development and tissue homeostasis. However, our understanding of this complex process remains incomplete. Methods: To identify new regulators of primary cilia formation or function, we carried out proximity labeling experiments and compared interactomes under ciliogenesis-restrictive and permissive conditions. Using an unbiased strategy, we selected candidates that were tested functionally by siRNA-mediated depletion or gene editing, in combination with gene expression analysis and various microscopy techniques, using either vertebrate cell lines or zebrafish as model systems. Results: We demonstrate that one of our identified candidates, protein SAMD4B, is associated with the centrosome and is required for Shh signaling in NIH3T3 cells and eye development in zebrafish. Our data implicate defective ciliary recruitment of Shh pathway regulators ARL13B and SMO as a plausible mechanism underlying the SAMD4B-mediated regulation of Shh signaling. Conclusions: Together, our data identify a previously unrecognized link between SAMD4B, a protein known to be associated with cytoplasmic RNA condensates, and ciliary signaling.

items.title: NeuroSim: a clinically informed multi-disorder EEG simulator with personalized pattern injection and AI-driven neurological modeling
items.abstract: Deep learning for electroencephalography (EEG) based neurodiagnostics is constrained by the limited availability of labeled clinical recordings. Datasets covering Alzheimers disease (AD), Parkinsons disease (PD), schizophrenia (SCZ), epilepsy (EPI), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are scarce, demographically narrow, and heterogeneous across acquisition sites, while privacy requirements restrict data sharing. Existing EEG simulators typically address a single disorder or trade biological interpretability for statistical fidelity. This study presents NeuroSim, a simulation framework that generates synthetic multichannel EEG with user-controlled injection of disease-specific patterns across five disorders and multiple severity levels. A physiologically motivated baseline generator produces band-limited rhythms, event-related potentials, artifacts, and hierarchical subject-level and trial-level variability. Disease patterns are introduced through region-specific and severity-specific spectral modulation that encodes established biomarkers, including posterior alpha suppression in AD, motor beta enhancement in PD, and spike-wave discharges in EPI. An interactive interface exposes montage, sampling rate, duration, artifacts, stimuli, affected regions, and severity, and exports signals with reproducible metadata. The simulated signals reproduced the expected biomarker directionality under spectral, topographic, and multivariate statistical analysis. A convolutional-attention classifier trained on simulated data reached 95.3 to 96.8 percent hold-out accuracy, and post hoc explainability analyses produced class-separable embeddings with attributions concentrated on pathophysiologically expected electrodes. Application of the analysis pipeline to recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus confirmed compatibility with heterogeneous clinical data. In subject-level augmentation experiments on real clinical EEG, supplementing real training data with NeuroSim samples increased classification accuracy from 91.6 to 94.5 percent for AD versus healthy controls and from 90.9 to 94.0 percent for PD versus healthy controls, exceeding the improvement obtained with conventional signal-level augmentation. NeuroSim is released as open-source software to support augmentation, benchmarking, and explainable artificial intelligence in neurological diagnostics.

items.title: Learning RNA secondary structure from chemical probing with MXfold2
items.abstract: Training RNA secondary structure predictors is limited by scarce reference annotations, even as chemical probing produces abundant nucleotide-level measurements. These measurements inform pairing states without identifying base-pairing partners. Here we extend MXfold2, which combines neural and thermodynamic folding scores, to learn from probing profiles and predict RNA secondary structures from sequence alone. We introduce three training objectives. One learns from probing-assisted target structures. The other two use implicit maximum-likelihood estimation to pass surrogate gradients from reactivity-ranking and likelihood losses through discrete folding. Simulations, RNAgym measurements and external structural tests show improved chemical agreement and gains in exact base-pair prediction when chemical supervision is combined with structural pretraining and replay. Probing profiles can thus broaden the range of RNAs that inform sequence-only structure prediction, including RNA populations with few complete structure annotations.

items.title: SNP2Cluster-Py: A pathogen-agnostic, context-aware framework for Core SNP and transmission-cluster analysis
items.abstract: Whole-genome sequencing enables high-resolution identification of genetically related pathogen isolates, but genomic similarity alone does not establish epidemiologically meaningful transmission. We developed SNP2Cluster-Py, an open-source Python framework that separates context-aware Core SNP clustering from the subsequent application of epidemiological and temporal criteria. The software accepts a precomputed pairwise Core SNP-distance matrix and user-configured metadata and supports analysis of all eligible isolates in a single context, as well as sequence-type, geographical, epidemiological and ordered composite contexts. Within each context, authoritative Core clusters are defined as connected components of an SNP-threshold graph; K-means assignments and silhouette widths are retained as exploratory diagnostics only. We evaluated the workflow using 172 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from six neonatal-surveillance hospitals in South Africa, a focused 36-isolate single-hospital subset from the same surveillance dataset, and 168 Streptococcus pneumoniae carriage isolates from Ghana. In the full K. pneumoniae dataset, ST-only analysis assigned 141 isolates to Core SNP clusters, whereas Facility + ST analysis assigned 134, demonstrating how facility stratification can remove cross-facility genomic connections. In the single-hospital subset, both contexts assigned 30 of 36 isolates to five Core clusters, and Facility analysis retained 23 isolates in four temporally compatible clusters. In the pneumococcal dataset, ST-context analysis assigned 114 isolates to 38 Core clusters, which were characterised across sampling locations and time through Community analysis. SNP2Cluster-Py therefore provides a reproducible framework for adapting genomic clustering to specific surveillance questions while maintaining a clear distinction between genomic relatedness, analytically inferred transmission clusters and confirmed direct transmission. SNP2Cluster-Py v1.1.2 is available under the Apache License 2.0 through GitHub and Zenodo.

items.title: CELL-X: A Single-Cell Transcriptomics Framework for Cell-Type and Disease-State Prioritization of Type 2 Diabetes Risk Genes
items.corresponding_institution: A.V. College of Arts, Science & Commerce (Autonomous), Osmania University
items.abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci associated with Type 2 Diabetes (T2D), yet pinpointing specific causal genes and their relevant cellular contexts remains a critical bottleneck. To address this gap, we developed CELL-X, a novel computational framework systematically integrating fine-mapped genetic evidence with high-resolution single-cell transcriptomics and disease progression dynamics. Utilizing a custom out-of-memory processing engine, we analyzed an integrated human pancreatic islet atlas of 245,878 cells without forced data downsampling. We evaluated 37 genetically supported T2D candidate genes, quantifying cell-type relevance via a max-scaled Cell Relevance Score (CRS). Disease-associated transcriptional dynamics were subsequently incorporated using a Disease Relevance Score (DRS) based on heterogeneous expression shifts across normal, prediabetic, and T2D metabolic states. CELL-X successfully identified beta cells as the dominant disease-relevant cellular context and prioritized established causal genes, including SLC30A8, GLIS3, GCK, and TCF7L2. Validation against a 30-gene benchmark demonstrated exceptional target recovery and significant metabolic pathway enrichment. Furthermore, rigorous statistical null modeling confirmed this prioritization is driven by true biological variance rather than background transcriptomic noise. Ultimately, CELL-X provides a highly scalable, robust framework for generating biologically informed hypotheses in complex polygenic disease research.

items.title: The tumor suppressor role of the KRAS proto-oncogene in metastatic pancreatic cancer.
items.abstract: KRAS is the most frequently mutated proto-oncogene in human cancers. Progression to advanced disease is frequently associated with allelic imbalance of the KRAS locus with gain of the mutant allele and loss of the wild-type allele through clonal and sub-clonal loss of heterozygosity (LOH). While a large body of literature has focused on the effects of allelic imbalance on oncogene addiction through gain of the mutant allele, the role of the wild-type KRAS proto-oncogene in malignant progression has not been fully elucidated. To capture this phenomenon, we developed a first-in-class somatic mosaic and lineage tracing genetically engineered mouse model (smGMLT) of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma allowing for real time in vivo tracing of Kras-LOH. Longitudinal characterization of the smGMLT demonstrated the presence of a strong evolutionary bottleneck towards the selective loss of the wild-type allele at metastatic sites. Cross species analysis leveraging research autopsies and surgical specimens revealed that KRAS-LOH is associated with metastatic dissemination and shorter overall survival. Transcriptomic analysis through single-cell RNA sequencing uncovered a conserved phenomenon whereby KRAS-LOH is paralleled by an immune evasive phenotype through loss of the tumor-cell interferon response and reduced CD8+ T cell infiltration. In line with this evidence, orthotopic transplants of isogenic tumor populations differing for the Kras allelic status demonstrated that only cancer cells with Kras-LOH are are able to form tumors in immune competent animals. Restoration of the wild-type allele abrogates tumorigenesis in KrasLOH transplants in immunocompetent through activation of the TBK1-IRF axis. Altogether, these studies demonstrate that the KRAS proto-oncogene is a functional tumor suppressor in pancreatic cancer exerting its function through interferon-mediated, cell-extrinsic modulation of the tumor immune microenvironment.

items.title: Spatial organization of a SPINK1-associated tumor-stromal ecosystem links metabolic remodeling to immune restriction in bladder cancer
items.corresponding_institution: School of Biopharmacy, China Pharmaceutical University, 639 Longmian Road, Nanjing 211198, China.
items.abstract: Spatially organized tumor-stromal interactions contribute to metabolic remodeling and immune suppression in bladder cancer (BLCA). Using spatial transcriptional programs to define single-cell states, we identified a niche comprising SPINK1-high epithelial cells (E2) and TPM2-high cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) (C1). SPINK1 promoted tumor growth and myofibroblastic CAF programs, with EGFR and TGF-{beta} signaling implicated in tumor-CAF communication. Inferred metabolic reactions and spatial metabolite distributions supported a candidate circuit linking tumor-derived lactate to CAF oxidative metabolism and glutamine provision, followed by tumor glutamine utilization for reductive carboxylation and fatty acid synthesis. SPINK1 perturbation altered extracellular glutamine and lactate concentrations. Predicted chemokine interactions implicated C2/C3 CAFs in T cell recruitment, whereas the E2-C1 niche exhibited checkpoint and exhaustion-associated features. RHCG-positive tumor regions contained higher proportions of TOXCXCR4 cells among CD3 T cells, suggesting a possible association between ammonia handling and T cell dysfunction. In vivo, Spink1 loss attenuated tumor progression, increased cytotoxic CD8 T-cell infiltration, and enhanced tumor control during PD-1 blockade. These findings identify a spatially organized tumor-stromal niche associated with metabolic cooperation and immune restriction, supporting SPINK1 as a candidate therapeutic target in combination with immunotherapy.

items.title: Beta-cell-derived urocortin-3 contributes to glucose-regulated somatostatin and glucagon secretion in the mouse pancreas
items.abstract: Aims/Hypothesis. Glucagon secretion is impaired in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. The mechanisms behind this dysregulation are incompletely understood. Urocortin-3 (UCN-3), a beta-cell-derived peptide, stimulates somatostatin (SST) secretion and may thereby regulate glucagon secretion. We investigated the mechanisms through which UCN-3 regulates pancreatic hormone secretion and examined the physiological contribution of endogenous UCN-3 to glucose-regulated hormone secretion. Methods. Pancreatic hormone secretion was studied using the isolated perfused mouse pancreas. The effects of exogenous and endogenous UCN-3 were investigated using selective antagonists of SST receptors (SSTR) and corticotropin-releasing hormone receptor 2 (CRHR2). In addition, the role of UCN-3 was examined in streptozotocin (STZ) treated mice. Results. Exogenous UCN-3stimulated somatostatin secretion and inhibited glucagon secretion in the mouse pancreas. Blockade of SSTRs completely abolished the glucagonostatic effect of UCN-3, demonstrating that inhibition of glucagon secretion is indirectly mediated through SST signaling. Moreover, CRHR2 antagonism prevented both UCN-3-induced SST secretion and inhibition of glucagon secretion, identifying CRHR2 as the key receptor mediating these effects. During acute glucose stimulation (3.5-10mM), CRHR2 antagonism reduced glucose-induced stimulation of SST and attenuated glucagon inhibition, indicating that endogenous UCN-3 participates in the acute islet response to hyperglycemia. However, during sustained hyperglycemia, CRHR2 antagonism reduced SST secretion without altering glucagon secretion. In STZ-treated mice, glucose-induced SST secretion was lost. Conclusions. Urocortin-3 regulated glucagon secretion indirectly through CRHR2-dependent stimulation of SST secretion. Endogenous UCN-3 contributes to the acute islet response to hyperglycemia, supporting a physiologically relevant beta-cell-to-delta-cell-to-alpha-cell paracrine axis in the mouse pancreas. This pathway is disrupted following beta-cell loss, suggesting a potential contribution to impaired islet hormone regulation in diabetes.

items.title: Palmitic acid overload does not promote full-blown dysfunction in SGBS adipocytes which is reflected in their secretome
items.abstract: Background: Energy excess, and particularly long-chain saturated fatty acid (SFA) overload, are instrumental in promoting obesity and hampering metabolic health. However, SFA contribution to human adipocyte metabolic and endocrine dysfunction remains elusive. Nonetheless, we have already provided evidence that a 48-hour palmitic acid (PA) exposure is not sufficient to hamper Simpson-Golabi Behmel Syndrome (SGBS) adipocytes insulin signalling. Objective: This study aims at evaluating whether a 96-hour exposure to PA is able to disrupt SGBS adipocyte metabolic health and induce the release of a secretome capable of hampering insulin signalling in skeletal muscle cells. Methods: SGBS adipocytes were treated with either 1000 uM PA or bovine serum albumin (BSA) for 96 hours followed by the assessment of the NFkB signalling and the expression of genes associate with inflammation and adipocyte metabolic stress. Furthermore, adipocytes were labelled with BODIPY and lipid droplet as well as cell size semi-quantified using ImageJ. Insulin-induced phosphorylation of Akt and Akt substrate of 160 kDa (AS160) was assessed by Western Blot. The effect of PA on SGBS secretome was assessed by both ELISA as well as MILLIPLEX. Finally, human immortalised myotubes were co-cultured with BSA or PA-treated SGBS adipocytes for 24 hours followed by the assessment of insulin signalling at the Akt level. Results: PA did not activate the NFkB signalling pathway, but induced the expression of MCP-1 while tending to upregulate IL-6 mRNA levels. Despite 96-hour PA exposure leading to an increase in lipid droplet and cell size, this was not coupled with an impairment in insulin signalling. Nevertheless, this SFA promoted an increase in IL-6 and IL-8 secretion while tending to enhance the release of adiponectin by SGBS adipocytes. Finally, the secretome from PA-treated SGBS adipocyte did not impair insulin-induced phosphorylation of Akt relative to controls in myotubes. Conclusions: Thus, in the absence of the stromal vascular fraction, direct exposure of SGBS adipocytes to PA overload is not sufficient to elicit overt dysfunction. The absence of full-blown adipocyte dysfunction is reflected in the secretome of these cells which failed to disrupt skeletal muscle insulin signalling.

items.title: Comparative transcriptomics reveals shared and context-dependent adaptations of bovine cells across culture systems for cultivated meat
items.corresponding_institution: The Department of Animal Sciences, Robert H. Smith Faculty of Agriculture, Food, and Environment,  The Hebrew University of Jerusalem,  Rehovot 7610001, Israel
items.abstract: Developing cell-culture systems for cultivated meat requires understanding how candidate cells respond to prolonged expansion and different growth environments. However, the extent to which bovine cells share transcriptional adaptations across these conditions, or retain responses specific to their origin and cellular state, remains unclear. Here, we systematically profiled bovine umbilical cord (BUC)- and adipose tissue (BAT)-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) across different culture architectures, passage stages, and differentiation states, including immortalized BUC cells and satellite cells as a myogenic reference. We show that global transcriptomic variation is strongly associated with culture architecture, cell identity, and cellular state. Immortalization preserved several early-passage transcriptional features, particularly proliferation-related programs, while opposing selected changes associated with primary cell aging. Culture architecture induced distinct rather than uniform three-dimensional responses. Spheroid formation produced a pronounced transcriptional shift characterized by reduced proliferation-, chromatin-, and development-associated programs, alongside changes in extracellular-matrix organization, metabolism, and intracellular remodeling. Across primary umbilical cord-derived, adipose-derived, and myogenically induced umbilical cord-derived cells, scaffold-versus-plate comparisons revealed correlated but non-identical transcriptional responses. These involved changes in extracellular-matrix organization, adhesion, membrane trafficking, and developmental pathways, with endocytosis enriched across all three comparisons among the pathways examined. During myogenic induction, both satellite cells and BUC-derived cells exhibited muscle-related cytoskeletal and contractile programs, while scaffold culture further supported myogenic signatures in BUC-derived cells. These findings distinguish recurring culture-associated responses from transcriptional features tied to cell source and expansion history. They support evaluating cultivated-meat candidate cells in their intended culture systems, not solely under conventional plate conditions.

items.title: Large-scale Nanopore sequencing resolves species diversity and distribution of European Ulva
items.abstract: The green algal genus Ulva is widespread and ecologically important in European coastal ecosystems. However, species diversity and distributions remain poorly resolved due to phenotypic plasticity and historical taxonomic uncertainty. By adopting a large-scale sampling and barcoding effort, we provide a unique continent-scale assessment of Ulva species diversity and distribution. We developed a novel high-throughput Oxford Nanopore Technologies sequencing strategy, pooling 768 samples (eight 96-well plates) per run and sequencing tufA and ITS simultaneously. Nanopore barcoding was accurate and efficient, with 96.3% of samples yielding at least one informative marker. Consensus sequences showed 99.4-100% similarity to Sanger sequences. By analysing 3,657 samples from 30 countries, we identified 46 species with contrasting distribution patterns and substantially expanded their known geographic ranges. This includes numerous country-level first records and the first records of Ulva howensis outside Australia and U. meridionalis within the study area. Five non-indigenous Ulva species were also detected, including widespread occurrences of U. australis. However, 10 species could not be assigned to named taxa because suitable reference sequences were unavailable or unreliable, highlighting persistent taxonomic gaps in public databases. Our findings demonstrate the power of coordinated, high-throughput molecular surveys to resolve cryptic marine biogeography at continent scales. The resulting high-resolution spatial baseline facilitates the early detection of non-indigenous species and range expansions. It also enables coastal managers to monitor invasion pathways, evaluate ecosystem risks associated with opportunistic bloom-forming taxa, and detect climate-driven distribution shifts across European waters.

items.title: ChIP-seq analysis of SMAD3 target genes in a sea anemone reveals symbiosis-dependent regulation through TGF-β signaling
items.abstract: Background: Cnidarian-algal symbiosis underpins coral reefs, but elevated temperatures can disrupt it, causing bleaching. Bleaching activates host stress and immune pathways and disrupts symbiotic signaling and nutrient transfer. Among these pathways, the immunosuppressive cytokine transforming growth factor-{beta} (TGF-{beta}) promotes host tolerance of symbionts in cnidarians, but the genes regulated by its transcription factor, SMAD3, remain unknown. SMAD3 ChIP-seq and RNA-seq were used to identify putative targets in symbiotic and aposymbiotic Exaiptasia diaphana after 6 and 18 h of heat stress. Results: SMAD3 binding was highly specific to each combination of symbiotic state and heat treatment. Symbiotic state, not heat stress, drove most differential binding, with binding nearly always higher in symbiotic animals. Integration identified 625 putative targets differentially bound and expressed between symbiotic states. Differential binding between symbiotic states peaked at 18 h, when these targets made up the largest share of symbiosis-associated expression differences. Activation targets suggest SMAD3 supports symbiosis through the mucociliary surface, host control of nitrogen available to symbionts, uptake of symbiont-derived retinoids, and immunity. Repression targets, which outnumbered activation targets at 18 h, suggest SMAD3 limits canonical sterol transport, alters G protein-coupled receptor expression, and may reinforce its own activity by repressing negative regulators of TGF-{beta} signaling. Conclusions: SMAD3 appears to act as a bifunctional regulator whose binding is shaped primarily by symbiotic state. Its putative targets suggest roles in cnidarian symbiosis beyond immune suppression, including nutrient exchange and retinoid signaling. These findings provide a framework for TGF-{beta} function in cnidarian symbiosis and thermal stress.

items.title: 2-hydroxyglutarate-dependent inhibition of TET2 is a molecular link between metabolic reprogramming and smooth muscle cell differentiation
items.corresponding_institution: The University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston
items.abstract: Background: Smooth muscle cell (SMC) phenotypic modulation is accompanied by metabolic reprogramming, but the mechanisms linking metabolism to contractile gene expression remain unclear. We investigated whether 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), an inhibitor of ?-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, links metabolic changes to regulation of ten-eleven translocation 2 (TET2) in Acta2R179C/+ SMCs Methods: Primary wild-type (WT) and Acta2R179C/+ mouse aortic SMCs were treated with nicotinamide riboside (NR), exogenous R&L-2-HG, or cholesterol. Endogenous accumulation of L-2HG was achieved by lentivuris-mediated knockdown (KD) of L2hgdh. We assessed contractile marker expression, cellular metabolism, TET2 chromatin occupancy, and DNA methylation and hydroxymethylation. L-2HG levels were assessed using liquid chromatography/mass spectroscopy. Carotid artery 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) staining was assessed in mice after left carotid artery ligation. Results: Acta2R179C/+ SMCs have elevated 2-HG, reduced TET2 expression and chromatin occupancy, and lower 5hmC enrichment at CArG-containing SMC loci, consistent with repressed TET2 activity. NR boosts oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), reduces 2-HG in WT and mutant SMCs, increases TET2 expression and 5hmC enrichment, and reduces global 5-methylcytosine. Carotid artery 5hmC staining shows changes in the same direction, but group differences are not statistically significant. Exogenous L-2-HG attenuates NR-induced contractile marker expression in Acta2R179C/+ SMCs and also decreases contractile marker expression, reduces TET2 occupancy and 5hmC enrichment, and shifts WT SMC metabolism toward glycolysis, phenocopying the metabolic state of Acta2R179C/+ SMCs. Endogenous accumulation of L-2HG by L2hgdh KD reduces contractile markers in WT SMCS. Cholesterol reduces TET2 and contractile marker expression, decreases 5hmC enrichment, and increases global DNA methylation. Conclusions: These findings support a role for 2-HG in coupling metabolic state to epigenetic changes associated with SMC phenotypic modulation. NR-associated differentiation coincides with increased TET2 expression and DNA hydroxymethylation, identifying metabolic regulation of the SMC epigenome as a potential approach to preserving contractile gene expression.

items.title: The genetic architecture of lipoprotein(a): simplicity, complexity, and mutability
items.corresponding_institution: Brigham and Women's Hospital and Harvard Medical School
items.abstract: High levels of lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)) increase risk of cardiovascular diseases. Lp(a) concentration is primarily determined (>80%) by genetic variation at LPA, particularly by its large, size-polymorphic kringle IV-2 (KIV-2) repeat. However, because variation of the KIV-2 repeat is difficult to measure, the precise ways that genetic variants at LPA and other loci determine Lp(a) levels have been unclear, especially in individuals of non-European ancestry. Here, we developed new computational techniques to accurately genotype KIV-2 variation in whole-genome-sequenced population cohorts. Applying these methods to UK Biobank (n=490,414) and All of Us (n=245,394) provided insights into the genetic determinants of Lp(a) and the mutational dynamics of the KIV-2 repeat, which we found expands or contracts intra-allelically once every [~]500 generations. Variation in Lp(a) levels among people of all genetic ancestries was accurately predicted by a single, transferable genetic model capturing cis-epistatic effects of KIV-2 length and protein-altering polymorphisms in LPA. Controlling for predicted effects of LPA alleles revealed an additional, highly polygenic contribution to Lp(a) variation: LPA-adjusted Lp(a) levels associated with genetic variation at over 300 loci (P<5x10-8), much like other blood lipids. These results elucidate the genetic architecture and mutational origins of Lp(a) variation, showing how detailed characterization of a largely monogenic trait can provide surprising insights for complex trait genetics.

items.title: Improving Target-Adverse Event Association Prediction via Inverse Node Frequency Transformation to Mitigate Knowledge Graph Topological Bias
items.abstract: Motivation: Identifying significant associations between therapeutic protein targets and adverse events (AEs) is a critical component of drug safety assessment. To accelerate the process, machine learning methods have been developed to predict these associations as edges in network data integrating molecular interactions and other key biomedical knowledge. However, these networks often suffer from topological imbalances where a minority of "hub" nodes determine the predictive signal. This "topological" or "degree bias" can lead to poor performance on novel or understudied targets where safety inference is most needed. Results: We introduce Inverse Node Frequency (INF), a generally applicable node degree-based approach for mitigating topological bias. Employing an enriched biomedical knowledge graph and our own carefully curated target-adverse event associations, we apply INF as a normalisation procedure on a class of graph-derived features called metapaths and evaluate their resulting target-AE association prediction performance. Our results demonstrate that INF significantly improves the true positive rate (TPR/recall) for low-degree targets compared to the untransformed metapath features as well as a popular established normalisation method, while also achieving highly competitive hits@k, a ranking-based metric for knowledge graph-based inference. We also evaluated INF on an external set of target-AE associations never before used for modelling, on which INF also showed superior resilience compared to the two benchmarks.

items.title: TEAD Palmitoylation Inhibitors are Brain Penetrant and Enhance Survival in Preclinical Models of Recurrent Glioblastoma in Combination with Standard-of-Care Therapy
items.corresponding_institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose: Oncogenic addiction to YAP-TEAD signaling drives adaptive plasticity, therapeutic resistance, invasion and tumor progression in many cancers, including in glioblastoma (GBM), and represents an actionable vulnerability to explore as adjuvant therapy during tumor recurrence. This study evaluated the translational potential of orally bioavailable Vivace Therapeutics (VT) TEAD palmitoylation inhibitors in preclinical GBM models. Experimental Design: The effects of VT103 and VT104 on GBM proliferation, migration, and TEAD activity were first assessed across patient-derived GBM cell lines with diverse genomic drivers. The drugs pharmacokinetics (PK) and biodistribution were measured using mass spectrometry in mice bearing patient-derived orthotopic xenograft (PDX) GBM. Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated in two genetically distinct PDX models of recurrent GBM, administering VT104 as monotherapy or in combination with standard-of-care radiotherapy plus temozolomide (RT+TMZ). Results: VT104/VT103 treatment significantly impaired GBM proliferation and migration in-vitro, with concomitant downregulation of TEAD-target expression. PK studies confirmed sustained VT104 plasma levels and robust brain biodistribution in PDX mice, with brain:plasma ratio >150% at therapeutic dosing without systemic toxicity. While VT104 monotherapy showed modest anti-tumor effects, combination therapy (VT104+RT+TMZ) significantly extended overall survival in both recurrent GBM PDX models. The survival benefit was most prominent in EGFR-mutant GBM and corresponded to significant decrease in overall and infiltrative tumor burden. Mechanistically, VT104 potentiated TMZ-dependent {gamma}-H2AX genotoxic stress and RT+TMZ synergized with VT104 to abolish TEAD activity. Conclusion: Integrating YAP-TEAD inhibition with standard therapy introduces a clinically-relevant paradigm for synergistic treatment in recurrent GBM that both inhibits tumor infiltration and reduces therapeutic resistance to chemoradiation.

items.title: Multiple isoforms of cancer stemness regulator NanogP8 in clinical prostate cancer specimens and their unique biochemical and oncogenic properties
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Pharmacology & Therapeutics, Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center, Elm & Carlton Streets, Buffalo, NY 14263, USA
items.abstract: The pluripotency regulator Nanog (NANOG, for human protein) has been reported to be overexpressed in cancers and in cancer stem cells (CSCs). We have previously shown that NanogP8, encoded by one of the expressed Nanog pseudogenes, is the predominant transcript expressed in several cancers including prostate cancer (PCa). We have also demonstrated that NanogP8 is functionally important in tumorigenesis as its loss impairs tumor regeneration and growth while inducible expression of NanogP8 is sufficient to reprogram androgen-dependent PCa to an androgen-independent and castration-resistant state. In the current study, we combined RT-PCR, subcloning and sequencing to systematically analyze the open reading frame sequences of Nanog and NanogP8 mRNA transcripts in treatment-naive clinical human PCa (HPCa) specimens. Our results revealed that HPCa did not express the ES cell-specific Nanog1 mRNA but primarily expressed NanogP8 together with several other Nanog pseudogenes including NanogP7 and NanogP6. Interestingly, most HPCa specimens contained multiple isoforms of NanogP8 transcripts, and we identified novel missense mutations in the NanogP8 transcripts that could lead to amino acid changes. Experiments with recombinant proteins, site-directed mutagenesis and Western blotting revealed several mutations that conferred the NanogP8 variant proteins, including NanogP8L61P, NanogP8D64Y, and NanogP8N130S, with unique biochemical properties. Moreover, some mutations furnish NanogP8 isoforms with distinct CSC and oncogenic characteristics. Altogether, this study advances our knowledge of the molecular, biochemical and oncogenic properties of Nanog expression and NanogP8 isoforms in PCa.

items.title: Spatial co-enrichment of immature myeloid and T-cell populations predicts survival in NPM1-mutant AML
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Pathology and Neuropathology, University Hospital and Comprehensive Cancer Center Tuebingen, Tuebingen, Germany
items.abstract: NPM1-mutant acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is the most common molecularly defined AML subtype. Outcomes vary considerably across co-mutational profiles, and the bone marrow (BM) microenvironment may shape treatment responses through immune cell interactions. Whether these interactions form spatially organized structures with independent prognostic relevance in the diagnostic BM is unknown. We used CO-Detection by indEXing (CODEX) with a 54-marker panel and MERFISH spatial transcriptomics to profile 67 NPM1-mutant AML patients at diagnosis and 38 age- and sex-matched normal BM (NBM) controls on tissue microarrays from archival FFPE samples, profiling 1,494,397 cells and annotating 27 cell types. Compared to NBM, NPM1-mutant AML showed striking architectural reorganization, including a loss of stroma association with adaptive immune cells and loss of NBM-specific mature myeloid and erythroid cellular neighborhoods. AML was characterized by expansion of phenotypically distinct immature myeloid (IM) populations with aberrant immunophenotypes, including CD11b+ VISTA+ and CD15+ subsets, alongside an expansion of CD8+ and PD1+ CD4+ T-cells. While cell type and neighborhood cluster frequencies showed limited prognostic associations, spatial context-dependent interactions were more informative. Both enrichment of CD11b+ IM in adaptive immune neighborhoods, and co-enrichment with CD8+ T-cells were adversely associated with overall survival. Spatial transcriptomics identified upregulated genes associated with monocytic AML in CD11b+ IM cells and candidate immunosuppressive ligand-receptor interactions, including TGFB1-TGFBR1 and JAG1-NOTCH1, with T-cells. These findings indicate that spatial context of suppressor-immune cell interactions carries prognostic information not captured by genomics or cell type frequencies alone and is amenable to translation using routine diagnostic FFPE samples.

items.title: A deep-learning predictive model for Cas12a activity in wheat
items.corresponding_institution: VIB-UGent Center for Plant Systems Biology
items.abstract: CRISPR technology has created targeted DNA mutations across the tree of life. Target sites are defined by RNA molecules that largely determine the efficiency of an experiment. Several predictive models are available to select the most efficient RNAs. Unfortunately, these models are not built with plant data and have limited predictive power in plant systems. To overcome this limitation, we established a high-throughput arrayed wheat protoplast transfection method and measured the editing efficiency of ~1,000 unique LbCas12a crRNAs at on- and off-target sites. We trained different models by testing 40 deep learning architectures and found that a convolutional neural network model called 2CaP-5 displayed the best performance. While 2CaP-5 had moderate to strong predictive power in protoplasts, it did not generalize to Agrobacterium-mediated transformation. Despite this limitation, we demonstrate that 2CaP-5 can be re-trained with as few as 500 crRNAs. The use of such a small training set is advantageous for low-throughput experimental systems such as typically found in transgenic plant systems. We also used ~2,000 off-targets in the wheat subgenomes to investigate Cas12a specificity. Our dataset confirms previous observations regarding off-targets, specifically that single mismatches reduce indel efficiency provided they are adjacent to the PAM and that off-target activity can be largely prevented by three mismatches. Altogether, our results show that the 2CaP-5 model has moderate to strong predictive power for Cas12a crRNAs in wheat protoplasts and will serve as a useful foundation for predictive tools in other plant species.

items.title: CsrA-dependent RNA accessibility landscapes prioritize new mRNA and sRNA targets and link CsrA to polyphosphate homeostasis
items.abstract: The global RNA-binding protein CsrA (Carbon Storage Regulatory Protein A) regulates diverse physiological processes in Gammaproteobacteria, but the full set of RNAs through which it actuates and how they intersect with small RNA (sRNA) regulation and stress physiology remain incompletely defined. We asked how CsrA shapes RNA accessibility across 431 untranslated mRNA regions and 87 sRNAs in Escherichia coli. Using a previously published RNA accessibility profiling method (INTERFACE), we compared wild type and CsrA mutant (csrA::kan) strains. Permissive screening for accessibility peaks at GGA/AGA motifs nominated 87 5'UTRs, 32 3'UTRs and 28 sRNAs as candidate responsive RNAs but did not pass a permutation null (p=0.43), however it can be used to guide selection of candidates for validation. Eleven 5'UTRs had no prior experimental evidence, and all 3'UTRs and most sRNAs were nominated manually because of limited probe numbers in these targets. In reporter assays, six of nine RNAs tested showed CsrA-dependent expression (mdtE, ribB, patA, metC, ppk and proS) including three candidate activated-targets, although only two of five reporters from the primary candidate list responded. CsrA bound the sRNAs SsrA and RalA in vitro, and reporter assays suggested CsrA-dependent modulation of previously identified ArrS-ribB and GcvB-crp interactions. Mutating sequence elements in the ppk 5' UTR altered CsrA-dependent expression, and loss of CsrA-activity was associated with reduced polyphosphate and fewer Hfq-containing HP-bodies during nitrogen starvation. Together, these findings expand the CsrA regulon and its overlap with sRNA networks, and support accessibility profiling to prioritize RNA-binding protein targets for follow-up characterization.

items.title: A differential-trend-subtype strategy for integrated serum proteomics and N-glycoproteomics reveals ovarian cancer-associated remodelling
items.abstract: Protein glycosylation is increasingly implicated in cancer, but its macro- and microheterogeneity complicate cohort-scale resolution of disease-associated remodeling. Here we performed matched peptide-level proteomic (PEP) and intact N-glycopeptide (NGP) profiling of serum from 100 participants, comprising 23 healthy controls, 27 individuals with benign ovarian disease and 50 patients with ovarian cancer. We identified 12,634 intact NGPs with plausible linkages spanning 6,127 protein-site glycosites and 4,438 glycoproteins. We developed a Differential-Trend-Subtype (DTS) target-prioritization framework integrating ovarian cancer versus non-malignant differences, cross-sectional healthy-benign-cancer trends and within-cancer subtype effects. Independent PEP and NGP clustering supported two aligned molecular states, assigning 47 of 50 cancer samples concordantly. Among 171 subtype-associated NGPs, cluster 1-high (C1-high) features were more frequently fucosylated, whereas cluster 2-high (C2-high) features were more frequently sialylated. DTS strategy prioritized a more informative pool of candidate features. Under leakage-controlled nested resampling, the best exploratory diagnostic panel-comprising PON1, HP and C9 peptide features together with an IGHM N209 N-glycopeptide-achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.843+-0.026, whereas the best subtype panel-comprising C2 N621 and IGHG1 N180 N-glycopeptides together with SERPINA3-achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.997+-0.005. These findings demonstrate the utility of DTS for prioritizing candidate markers and reveal coordinated protein and site-specific N-glycan remodelling with potential relevance to ovarian cancer diagnosis and molecular stratification.

items.title: Diet-Induced Obesity is Associated with Sex-Dependent Cerebral Microvascular Changes and Cognitive Decline in Mice
items.corresponding_institution: Metabolic Research Laboratories, Institute of Metabolic Science, University of Cambridge
items.abstract: Metabolic diseases, including obesity and diabetes, are major risk factors for cognitive impairment and dementia, yet the underlying causal mechanisms remain unclear. Here we investigate whether this link is mediated by dysfunctional changes in cerebral microvessels. Using a multimodal longitudinal approach combining 3D light-sheet fluorescence microscopy, contrast-enhanced MRI and cognitive testing, we characterise structural, functional and behavioural changes to the brain microvasculature in a mixed-sex mouse model of diet-induced obesity (DIO). Our results reveal a striking sex-specific vulnerability to obesity-driven cerebrovascular dysfunction. Brains from male DIO mice exhibited reduced capillary diameter and volume in the frontal cortex, alongside decreased blood volume and accelerated cognitive decline over time in an object recognition task. Conversely, female DIO mice displayed compensatory capillary vasodilation and were protected against neurovascular and cognitive impairment. These findings link cerebral microvascular changes to obesity-associated cognitive decline, and identify sex-dependent differences in the cerebrovascular response to obesity.

items.title: MLE EEG Toolbox: A Personal AI Laboratory Assistant for Literature-Informed and Reproducible M/EEG Research
items.abstract: Electrophysiological research increasingly relies on complex analytical workflows, yet integrating methodological evidence, computational execution and reproducibility remains challenging. Here we introduce MLE EEG Toolbox, a framework for building a personal AI laboratory assistant for electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) research. The toolbox integrates locally deployed AI, natural-language-guided analysis, literature retrieval and methodological comparison, and reproducible computational workflows. A constrained language model translates research instructions into validated, researcher-approved operations, while literature-informed guidance supports parameter selection and protocol reconstruction. Computational provenance enables transparent inspection and replay of analytical workflows. The assistant achieved action-selection accuracies of 85.6% for EEG and 95.5% for MEG, while 142 cross-platform tests demonstrated close numerical agreement. Applications to public EEG and MEG datasets illustrated integrated spectral, network, decoding and source analyses. Running on standard personal computers without external AI APIs or token charges, MLE EEG Toolbox provides an accessible, researcher-controlled environment that connects methodological knowledge with reproducible electrophysiological analysis.

items.title: A CT-to-brain-atlas mapping framework using cranial base landmarks in marmosets
items.abstract: Objective. The common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), a small, experimentally tractable nonhuman primate, is increasingly used as a model for studying higher brain functions. However, substantial individual differences in its skull and brain limit the accuracy of stereotaxic coordinates. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of each animal improves accuracy but is costly. Computed tomography (CT) is easy to acquire and shows the skull and implanted devices, but not the brain. We therefore aimed to map CT images to a brain atlas without MRI of each animal. Approach. Six marmosets with both CT and MR images served as references. A target CT image was registered to a reference CT image and mapped to the atlas via the reference's MR image. For this CT-to-CT registration, we compared intensity-based registration with landmark-based registration using eight cranial base landmarks. We also averaged mappings across multiple references. Mapping error was measured against the mapping via the target's own MR image. Main results. With a single reference, landmark-based registration had a significantly smaller error than intensity-based registration. Averaging the mappings from five references improved the accuracy (0.45 mm), and five or more landmarks gave almost the same accuracy as all eight. Landmark-based registration also worked better on CT images from a different scanner and on postoperative CT images with implants (three and two marmosets, respectively). Using our new open-source software, Marmoset Atlas Mapper, we assigned Neuropixels recording sites to brain regions on postoperative CT, and the region boundaries were qualitatively consistent with boundaries in local field potential correlations. Significance. Cranial base landmarks and multiple references allow CT-to-atlas mapping with a submillimeter mean error without MRI of each animal, even with image artifacts or partly missing landmarks. This enables in vivo localization of implanted devices, including those in deep structures, facilitating studies of higher brain functions in marmosets.

items.title: Motor learning engages intrinsic plasticity in the human cortex
items.abstract: Learning is commonly explained by changes in synaptic strength. In animals, however, learning also engages intrinsic plasticity -- changes in how readily neurons convert synaptic input into firing. Its contribution to human learning has been unclear, because conventional non-invasive measures of cortical excitability primarily reflect synaptic strength. Here we used controllable-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation to estimate two biophysical indices of intrinsic excitability in human motor cortex, before and after motor training. Training produced signatures of increased intrinsic excitability, selectively in the cortical representation of the trained muscle, but not an untrained muscle. Individuals showing larger intrinsic excitability changes learned faster, independently of changes in motor-evoked potential amplitude, an index of synaptic excitability that increased following training but did not predict learning rate. An axon model reproduced the measured changes through small shifts in membrane excitability. These findings provide evidence that intrinsic plasticity is expressed in the intact human brain, and that it represents a behaviourally relevant component of learning-related cortical adaptation.

items.title: Translation of small ORFs in non-canonical RNAs provides resilience to heat shock stress
items.corresponding_institution: Centro Andaluz de Biologia del Desarrollo, Universidad Pablo de Olavide, CSIC, 41089, Dos Hermanas, Sevilla, Spain.
items.abstract: Background: Heat shock and other stress conditions severely challenge cell and organismal survival. Characterising and understanding the genome responses to heat shock is of increasing interest due to the accelerated impact of global warming. Under heat shock and other stress conditions, the translation of most canonical genes is reduced as part of a physiological response to improve cellular and organismal resilience. Heat shock proteins (HSPs) are among a minority of proteins whose expression increases during heat shock, working as chaperones and helping other proteins to maintain their tertiary structure. Results: In contrast to canonical genes, whose translation is dramatically suppressed under heat shock conditions, we find that the translation of small Open Reading Frames (smORFs), especially those in so-called long-noncoding, (or long noncanonical) RNAs (lncRNAs), remains at similar levels, and in some cases is enhanced under heat shock in Drosophila melanogaster. lncRNA translation under heat stress entails a 3' shift in the smORFs translated in a given lncRNA, a shift that may be favoured by non-canonical smORF translation mechanisms. We also characterise two smORFs with stress-enhanced translation, showing that their expression is up-regulated by the heat stress response pathway, and that their microproteins improve organism survival and resilience under heat shock. Conclusion: smORF and lncRNA translation is more resilient to heat shock than that of standard genes, and this smORF translation can increase organismal resilience to heat shock, potentially representing a new component of the HSF stress-response gene regulation pathway. The stress-resilient lncRNA translation entails a 3' shift in the position and translation levels of smORFs being translated, and while the full molecular mechanism of this shift is not known at the moment, we propose that it might take advantage of non-canonical aspects of polycistronic lncRNA translation.

items.title: Structural and Metabolic Insufficiency of the Blood-Brain Barrier Is Associated with Schizophrenia Penetrance
items.abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is a highly specialized vascular endothelial network tightly regulating peripheral influences on the brain. BBB endothelial cells (ECs) are mitochondrially rich compared to peripheral ECs, and mitochondrial function has been linked with the induction of BBB properties. In the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22qDS), a condition with heightened risk for schizophrenia (SZ), we demonstrated rescue of BBB properties by restoring mitochondrial function. Thus, we sought to understand if energetic and structural capacities of the BBB may influence the SZ penetrance seen in 22qDS. We differentiated induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from control, 22qDS individuals without SZ (22qDS(-)SZ), and 22qDS individuals with SZ (22qDS + SZ) into BBB-like cells (iBBB). We found that the iBBBs derived from 22qDS + SZ display considerable reductions in the rate of oxygen consumption as compared to 22qDS without (22qDS(-)SZ). Furthermore, 22qDS(-)SZ iBBB retain control-level barrier characteristics, including resistance to ionic flux, and enhanced tight junction and cytoskeletal properties. These phenotypes were further reinforced by RNA sequencing, which implicated several metabolic-, cytoskeletal-, and cell-cell adhesion-related differentially expressed genes, and ontological and gene-set enrichment phenotypes. Together, our functional and transcriptomic data indicate a dual compensation in metabolic and structural programs specific to the 22qDS subgroup lacking a SZ diagnosis. Thus, the penetrance of SZ in the BBB strongly associates with the capacity to maintain structural and metabolic phenotypes, representing a defining feature of 22qDS-related SZ pathophysiology. These findings bridge a gap in knowledge of molecular features which characterize differential phenotypes in the psychosis subtypes of 22qDS and address divergent BBB cell biology between individuals with and without SZ.

items.title: 5-Azacytidine alleviates Liver Fibrosis via modulation of TET1 and TET3 levels and restoration of global 5hmC
items.abstract: DNA methylation and demethylation processes play a pivotal role in the onset and progression of liver diseases. The ten-eleven translocase enzymes (TET1, TET2 and TET3) are key DNA demethylases that oxidise 5-methylcytosine (5mC) to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), thereby regulating the cellular epigenetic state. Dysregulated TET expression has been increasingly associated with hepatic pathology. In this study, we assessed the DNA hydroxymethylation status of fibrotic and regenerating livers and correlated these changes with TET protein expression in a CCl induced murine model of liver fibrosis. Fibrosis progression was accompanied by a progressive, stage-wise reduction in hydroxymethylation, assessed by 5hmC immunostaining, together with a corresponding decrease in TET1 and increase in TET3 protein levels detected by immunoblotting. TET1 immunostaining correlated with the pattern of 5hmC immunostaining in fibrotic liver tissue. Treatment with the epigenetic agent 5-Azacytidine (5-AZA) improved liver morphology and lowered serum AST and ALT activities. 5-AZA treatment restored 5hmC levels and TET1 expression while downregulating TET3 in total liver tissue. Complementary in vitro studies in mouse primary and human stellate cells (LX-2) corroborated an increase in TET3 that correlated with elevated 5hmC, both of which were attenuated in stellate cells treated with 5-AZA. The reduction in TET3 corresponded with decreased expression of fibrogenic markers; -smooth muscle actin and Collagen-I. Collectively, this study identifies a progressive loss of 5hmC during liver fibrosis and demonstrates that pharmacological modulation via an epigenetic agent restores 5hmC homeostasis and TET-associated hydroxymethylation, attenuating fibrotic remodelling. These findings support targeting the DNA methylation-demethylation axis, and TET regulation in particular, as a promising therapeutic avenue for liver fibrosis.

items.title: The genetic and environmental basis of hematopoietic chimerism in marmosets
items.abstract: Common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus) have a high rate of twinning during pregnancy and exhibit an unusual phenomenon whereby stem cells migrate between fetuses in utero. These cells are integrated into a growing sibling resulting in each individual being a chimera of self and sibling. We mapped the distribution of chimerism across 145 marmosets by amplicon sequencing, showing high levels of chimerism in lateral mesoderm-derived tissues. By integrating pedigree and clinical records with estimates of chimerism we identified litter size to be a major determinant of chimerism and lifespan and demonstrate that chimerism and litter size are both heritable traits. Using exome sequencing of ~400 marmosets we identified major loci associated with variation in litter size and chimerism. These findings have implications for our understanding of self- and non-self across evolutionary biology, immunity and medicine.

items.title: Optimization of mitochondrial membrane potential contributes to extended longevity of daf-2 mutants in C. elegans
items.abstract: Mitochondrial membrane potential is the charge difference across the inner mitochondrial membrane that is generated by the electron transport chain pumping protons from the mitochondrial matrix to the intermembrane space and is required for ATP synthesis, importing proteins into the mitochondria and movement of ions across the inner mitochondrial membrane. While a number of long-lived genetic mutants in C. elegans have been reported to have reduced mitochondrial membrane potential, increased mitochondrial membrane potential has also been associated with increased longevity. In this work, we examined the role of mitochondrial membrane potential in the long lifespan of daf-2 insulin/IGF-1 receptor mutants. We found that mitochondrial membrane potential exhibits a small but significant decrease in day 1 daf-2 mutants but a much greater decrease in day 8 daf-2 worms. We also examined the effect of genes and compounds that have been shown to alter mitochondrial membrane potential on daf-2 lifespan. Disruption of ucp-4, which increases mitochondrial membrane potential, decreased daf-2 lifespan without reducing wild-type longevity. Treatment with the mitochondrial uncoupling compound FCCP (carbonyl cyanide-p-trimethoxyphenylhydrazone), which decreases mitochondrial membrane potential, also decreased the longevity of daf-2 worms with no effect on wild-type lifespan. Combined, these results suggest that the altered mitochondrial membrane potential in daf-2 mutants contributes to their extended longevity and that their long lifespan is dependent on maintaining mitochondrial membrane potential within an optimum range.

items.title: scPACE: A Personalized Autoencoder for Cell Evolution in Single-Cell Transcriptomics
items.abstract: Single-cell studies increasingly profile large cohorts of individuals, measuring thousands of cells in each donor. These datasets contain information at two levels: variation among individual cells and among donors. Analyzing both levels requires methods that can learn cellular representations, infer cell and donor states, and account for cell types that may be missing in some donors. Existing methods partially address these tasks. We introduce scPACE, a hierarchical personalized variational autoencoder handling these tasks. scPACE learns a cell representation, a cell state, and then aggregates cells within each type of cell to infer a donor state. It also imputes missing cell types with confidence estimates. Across simulated cohorts and a developing mouse visual-cortex dataset, scPACE recovered held-out cell and donor states accurately while achieving efficient cell-type imputation and representation. scPACE provides a unified framework for learning phenotypes across cellular and donor scales in cohort-scale single-cell transcriptomics.

items.title: VEGABrain: a Visualizer of Enriched Gene Analysis for the developing human brain
items.corresponding_institution: Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte
items.abstract: RNA sequencing datasets are widely reused resources in developmental neuroscience, yet inspecting them spatially remains unclear and difficult. Here, we present VEGABrain, an openly accessible web tool that renders bulk RNA-seq onto brain cortical and subcortical atlas surfaces across five human developmental windows spanning the first trimester to adulthood. Beyond single-gene maps, VEGABrain contributes a composite per-region enrichment layer using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) scores precomputed for [~]19,000 gene sets drawn from Gene Ontology, Reactome, KEGG, BioCarta, the Human Phenotype Ontology and the MSigDB hallmark collection, and aggregated to a score for every gene set, developmental window and brain region. Furthermore, VEGABrain allows users to submit a custom gene list and obtain its ssGSEA map across development, computed on demand. VEGABrain is open source and requires no installation, offering easy-to-query expression throughout development and brain areas.

items.title: Modelling Phenotypic Assay Noise for Multivariable Biomarker Discovery using Deep Neural Networks
items.corresponding_institution: Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, University Health Network
items.abstract: Accurately predicting cancer drug response remains a major challenge in precision oncology. Although some therapies are guided by clinically-approved biomarkers, these markers often yield limited predictive value and are unavailable for many drugs. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning approaches trained on large-scale cancer cell line pharmacogenomic screens offer a promising route to more comprehensive response prediction, yet they generally assume that phenotypic readouts are measured without error. This assumption is problematic because viability-based drug response assays are inherently noisy, potentially causing models to learn experimental artefacts rather than biologically meaningful determinants of sensitivity. Here, we show that phenotypic measurement noise is present in four widely used cancer cell line screening datasets and introduce Deep Concordance Index Networks (DeepCINET), a deep learning framework that explicitly accounts for this noise. Across datasets, incorporating this noise-aware ranking strategy improves generalization across experimental conditions and to previously unseen samples. DeepCINET outperforms baseline models in multiple settings, with particularly notable gains in prioritizing the most drug-sensitive cell lines. Together, these results establish phenotypic assay noise as a critical and previously overlooked source of error in drug response modelling and provide a principled framework for noise-aware multivariable biomarker discovery.

items.title: PhageLysClass: Evidence-aware classification of phage lytic proteins using protein language models
items.abstract: Phage lytic proteins are promising antibacterial and biotechnological candidates, yet uncertain annotations, modular architectures, and class imbalance complicate sequence-based classification. We developed PhageLysClass, an evidence-aware framework for recognizing lytic proteins and distinguishing Endolysins, Depolymerases, and virion-associated lytic enzymes. From 442,329 unique phage sequences, including 11,867 evidence-supported positives, we defined distinct candidate non-target, unlabeled, and challenge populations. Seven supervised and two positive-unlabeled tasks were evaluated across factorial redundancy and train-test homology conditions, yielding 2,240 and 768 experiments, respectively. Redundancy reduction influenced generalization more strongly than homology separation, with non-additive interactions between them. ESM2-T30 consistently outperformed alternative representations and supported a hierarchical classifier achieving approximately 0.89 MCC under strict R30/S30 conditions in the selected, pre-refitting benchmark. Applied without retraining to 77,897 sequences across three collections, PhageLysClass combined predictions with physicochemical and geometric contextualization, highlighting Depolymerase-like candidates among structurally ambiguous proteins while distinguishing reference-supported assignments from extrapolation.

items.title: Spatial single cell multi-omics identifies divergent melanoma-cell states associated with metastatic outcomes in thin primary melanomas
items.corresponding_institution: Translational Cell & Tissue Research, Department of Imaging & Pathology, KU Leuven, Leuven, Belgium.; KU Leuven Institute for Single Cell Omics (LISCO), KU Leuv
items.abstract: Thin melanomas (Breslow thickness [≤]1 mm) generally have favorable outcomes, yet some metastasise, highlighting the need for biomarkers of progression. Here, we combined same-section single-cell spatial transcriptomics and proteomics to identify seven melanoma-cell states organized along two inferred trajectories sharing a common trunk, extending from an in situ epithelial-adjacent state through developmental stress to melanocytic differentiation before diverging into two lineages. Lineage 1 progressed through an IFN-associated stress intermediate state towards mesenchymal-invasive cells enriched in metastasizing tumors and associated with immune-hot neighborhoods, extracellular-matrix remodeling and angiogenesis, potentially supporting vascular mimicry and metastatic dissemination. Lineage 2 terminated in cohesive nevus-like cells retaining melanocytic features within relatively immune-cold neighborhoods and enriched in non-metastasizing tumors. We confirmed these associations using H&E-inferred spatial transcriptomics in an international multicentric cohort and independent bulk transcriptomic datasets in primary melanomas, linking spatially organized melanoma-cell programs to metastatic outcome and identifying potential biomarkers of progression in thin melanoma.

items.title: Biologically Guided Deep Learning for Personalized PSA Forecasting in Intermittent Prostate Cancer Therapy
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Computer Science, University of Minnesota, Twin Cities, MN, USA
items.abstract: Intermittent Androgen Deprivation Therapy (IADT) offers a promising management strategy for prostate cancer by alternating treatment periods with the aim of delaying castration resistance and mitigating side effects. An evolutionary rationale for treatment interruptions is to preserve treatment-sensitive cells that may competitively suppress resistant populations. However, designing optimal patient-specific treatment schedules remains challenging due to the complex dynamics of tumor evolution and the computational intensity of traditional mechanistic simulation models. Standard mathematical models have prespecified structures that may inadequately capture patient-specific tumor evolution, limiting Prostate Specific Antigen (PSA) forecasting accuracy and adaptation to new patient data. These limitations may reduce the effectiveness of treatment policies learned using these models. To address them, we present a domain-adapted machine learning framework that integrates biological constraints into the deep learning architecture and embeds historical biomarkers to act as a robust, computationally efficient neural surrogate for mechanistic simulations.
