These results suggest that microglia and microglial activation, independent of astrocyte reactivity and the broader inflammatory response, is neuroprotective in a late-stage tau-associated neurodegeneration model.

items.title: Tumor cell-intrinsic AHR sustains IFNγ responsiveness and durable CD8 T-cell-mediated melanoma control
items.corresponding_institution: Laboratory of Experimental Dermatology, Department of Dermatology, Otto-von-Guericke-University, Magdeburg, Germany
items.abstract: The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) regulates melanoma differentiation and progression, but its tumor cell-intrinsic role in T-cell immunotherapy remains incompletely understood. Since AHR promotes inflammation-induced melanoma dedifferentiation, we hypothesized that AHR deficiency would reduce resistance to adoptive CD8 T-cell therapy (ACT) targeting melanocytic differentiation antigens. Unexpectedly, AHR-deficient HCmel12 melanomas exhibited more frequent delayed resistance to CD8 ACT despite initially impaired tumor growth. To investigate potential underlying mechanisms, we examined the responses of AHR-competent and AHR-deficient melanoma cells to prolonged interferon-{gamma} (IFN{gamma}) exposure. AHR-deficient cells initially exhibited enhanced IFN{gamma}-responsive transcription but progressively lost responsiveness during chronic stimulation, accompanied by reduced MHC class I and II surface expression. Transcriptomic analyses revealed a decline in IFN{gamma}-responsive gene expression and reduced expression of JAK/STAT signaling components, including JAK1. Treatment with the DNA methyltransferase inhibitor decitabine partially restored MHC expression, suggesting a potential contribution of epigenetic regulation. Despite their impaired responsiveness to prolonged IFN{gamma} exposure, AHR-deficient melanoma cells remained susceptible to alternative inflammatory cytotoxic mechanisms. Importantly, CD4 ACT, which can engage broader anti-tumor effector mechanisms, eradicated AHR-deficient melanomas. Together, these findings identify an unexpected role of tumor cell-intrinsic AHR in sustaining IFN{gamma} responsiveness during prolonged inflammatory exposure and reveal distinct outcomes of CD8- and CD4 T-cell-mediated melanoma control.

items.title: The MHC requirement for αβ T-cell specification is heterochronically gated
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Microbiology and Immunology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48109, USA
items.abstract: Major histocompatibility complex (MHC)-dependent thymic selection is a defining principle of {beta} T-cell development, yet mice lacking {beta}2m-dependent MHC class I and MHC class II retain rare {beta} T cells whose developmental significance has remained unresolved. Here we show that this residual compartment is not simply the product of failed selection. Single-cell and clonotypic profiling resolves distinct outcomes, including clonally restricted CD4-associated states and a diversified CD8 {beta} T-cell population that converges on physiological wild-type virtual memory. These CD8 cells lack conventional self-MHC calibration, retain broad T-cell receptor (TCR) diversity, respond rapidly to T-cell receptor and cytokine stimulation, and confer protection during bacterial infection. Their preservation is developmentally restricted: the MHC-independent state carries a neonatal transcriptional and phenotypic imprint, is favored by fetal but not adult progenitors, and is reduced by neonatal Lin28 inhibition. While these data do not displace the central requirement for MHC in generating the conventional naive {beta} T-cell repertoire, they establish that {beta} T-cell specification can proceed during early life in its absence, yielding a physiological and functionally competent CD8 {beta} T-cell fate. Thus, the MHC requirement for {beta} T-cell specification is heterochronically gated.

items.title: Mutations in core Ccr4-NOT subunits manifest links to decapping rather than deadenylation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
items.abstract: The mRNA polyadenosine tail (pA-tail) is gradually shortened in the cytoplasm by two main deadenylase complexes, Ccr4-NOT and Pan2/3, eventually leading to decapping and decay. The yeast Ccr4-NOT complex contains two deadenylases, Ccr4 and Pop2, and seven non-catalytic subunits. The functions of the latter are not yet fully understood. Here, we investigate the role of Ccr4-NOT in RNA metabolism in budding yeast. We show that steady-state mRNA pA-tail lengths increase with growth temperature, with this effect enhanced in ccr4{Delta} and pop2{Delta} cells, indicating a role for Ccr4-NOT in temperature-dependent mRNA regulation. Consistent with a functional divergence between species, we confirm that Ccr4 is the predominant deadenylase in yeast, whereas the Pop2 orthologs CNOT7/8 are the major deadenylases in human cells. Using Illumina and direct RNA sequencing, we characterize yeast strains defective in Ccr4-NOT, Pan2/3, or mRNA decapping. Unexpectedly, we show that loss of NOT1, NOT2, NOT4 or POP2 causes transcriptome and pA-tail changes resembling those of the decapping-factor mutants dhh1{Delta} and lsm1{Delta}, rather than of the principal deadenylase mutant ccr4{Delta}, and induces a mild stress response. Loss of Not2 or Not4 prolongs the half-lives of several mRNAs and causes growth defects comparable to decapping co-factor mutants. The mRNAs stabilized by loss of Not1-2-4 are distinct from those preferentially deadenylated by Ccr4-Pop2, suggesting different substrate targeting by Ccr4-NOT for non-overlapping functions in deadenylation and decapping.

items.title: Endogenous activation of multiple stress-response pathways during meiosis promotes gamete fitness
items.abstract: Gametogenesis, the process of meiosis coupled to gamete formation, transforms diploid progenitor cells into haploid gametes through extensive cellular remodeling and rewiring of gene expression. Several stress-responsive transcription factors (TFs) are upregulated during gametogenesis, but whether the cellular mechanisms that handle environmental stress also support the success of this developmental process is largely unexplored. Here, we show that four stress-responsive TFs, Hsf1, Skn7, and the paralogs Msn2 and Msn4, are endogenously active during budding yeast gametogenesis in the absence of external stress and drive distinct gene expression programs. Simultaneous meiotic depletion of Msn2, Msn4, and Skn7 compromise the fitness of the resulting gametes. We identified just two TF-dependent targets, the antioxidant genes TSA1 and AHP1, as important for gamete fitness, directly connecting TF activity to the protection of meiotic progeny. Our results demonstrate that the activation of canonical stress-response regulators is built into the meiotic program and suggest that such pathways can be repurposed during development to safeguard cellular health.

items.title: Loss of SRF-driven contractility, not lymphatic smooth muscle cell loss, is the primary driver of age-associated collecting vessel decline
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine, University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany
items.abstract: The lymphatic vasculature returns interstitial fluid to the blood circulation, a function that depends on rhythmic contraction of the smooth muscle cells (SMCs) surrounding collecting vessels. Lymph transport declines with age, a decline attributed largely to loss of SMCs from collecting vessels. We show that the principal change is not their loss but the loss of their contractile phenotype. In mouse ear collecting vessels, contractile protein expression declined with age and the vessels dilated, yet the majority of SMCs remained on the vessel wall. The decline extended to serum response factor (SRF), the transcription factor driving the smooth muscle contractile gene programme, and was mirrored by a loss of SRF-dependent contractile transcripts in published single-cell data from aged lymphatic muscle cells. Inducible deletion of Srf in mural cells reproduced this state, abolishing the contractile programme while leaving the cells in place and thereby excluding impaired SMC recruitment as the main mechanism. The resulting vessels became severely dilated and misshapen, whereas lymphatic capillaries were unaffected; endothelial identity, valve formation and lymphatic endothelial cell (LEC) number were all preserved, with enlargement instead reflecting increased LEC size. Intravital imaging showed loss of both rhythmic contraction and the contractile movement of individual SMCs, and Evans blue drainage to the inguinal lymph node was correspondingly reduced. Deletion of Srf after the contractile phenotype was established recapitulated this loss, showing that SRF is required continuously to maintain lymphatic SMC contractility and providing a genetic model of age-associated lymphatic dysfunction.

items.title: Inactive X chromosome DNA methylation erosion with age in human dermal fibroblasts
items.corresponding_institution: Altos Labs - Institute of Science, Cambridge, UK & Epigenetics Programme, Babraham Institute, Cambridge, United Kingdom & Department of Physiology, Development
items.abstract: X chromosome inactivation is an epigenetic process that establishes dosage compensation between the sexes through the monoallelic silencing of one X chromosome in karyotypically normal females. The allele that becomes inactivated is determined randomly during early development, resulting in females being mosaic with respect to whether the maternal or paternal allele is inactivated. This mosaicism makes it technically challenging to separate the active and inactive chromosomes in bulk populations, and consequently it has been historically difficult to study X chromosome inactivation in human cells. Here we use long read sequencing of 31 single cell clones derived from primary human dermal fibroblasts from 7 donors aged 25-80 years, and generate a method to distinguish DNA methylation state of the active versus the inactive X chromosome. As expected, CpG islands (CGIs) on the inactive X chromosome have high levels of methylation, while CGIs on the active X chromosome are very lowly methylated. Notably, we observe substantial loss of DNA methylation across multiple CGIs on the inactive X chromosome in an age dependent manner. We also observe this DNA methylation erosion in bulk samples by quantifying CGI methylation levels across individual sequencing reads. The genes that show age-related erosion of CGI methylation are associated with increased total transcription suggesting this methylation erosion generates a transcriptional permissive state. Overall, our study provides evidence of erosion of X chromosome inactivation with age in cell lines derived from primary human samples and implicates a role for loss of DNA methylation in the increased dosage of X chromosome linked genes in females with age. These findings shed new light on the epigenetic instability of the inactive X chromosome during human ageing and may be linked to age-related cellular dysfunction in females.

items.title: Large-scale 3D stitching montage cryo-electron tomography reveals heterogeneity and connectivity of lamellipodial actin networks
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Science and Technology Austria
items.abstract: Cellular processes range from local interactions among a few proteins to micrometer-scale assemblies whose coordinated components give rise to emergent properties. A prime example is the actin cytoskeleton in protrusive structures at the leading edge of migrating cells, termed lamellipodia. Significant progress has been made in understanding the functional contributions of distinct actin-filament populations and associated proteins within lamellipodia. Yet, a detailed quantitative appreciation of how actin filaments form a spatially connected and interdependent network has been impeded by limitations of existing methods. Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) can visualize such biological entities at molecular resolution in native cellular environments, but its limited field-of -view constrains quantitative analysis of extended assemblies. Hence, how lamellipodial actin architectures collectively support productive migration is not completely understood. Here, we present a 3D stitching montage cryo-ET workflow that advances both methodological and biological frontiers through its application to lamellipodia. We combine large-area montage-tilt series acquisition with independent tile reconstruction, denoising, and optical flow-based three-dimensional stitching to reconstruct large regions of the leading edge up to ~ 100 m2 at single-filament resolution. Bridging molecular resolution and cellular-scale context allows comprehensive filament tracing and quantification of actin filament networks, providing parameters for models of force generation in motile cells. Our data reveal that the network architecture in a seemingly uniform protrusive lamellipodium is markedly heterogeneous. By mapping Arp2/3 branch junction-based connectivity, using the molecular resolution of our data, we show how branch-junction distribution and network connectivity vary as a function of filament density and distance from the leading edge. We also identify the complex coexistence of short, branched and long, unbranched filament assemblies. We provide montage 3D volumes and filament vectorizations through an interactive, open web-based resource for browsing and interrogating the data. Our work thus provides a quantitative reference for lamellipodial actin architecture and a scalable approach for large-scale cryo-ET.

items.title: A genetic toolkit of visible mutants for Caenorhabditis briggsae
items.abstract: Caenorhabditis briggsae is a widely used model for comparative genetic studies involving C. elegans. Genetic analysis in C. briggsae depends on mutations with clear, easily recognizable phenotypes, yet most mutants reported so far have been mentioned only as names and linkage groups, without underlying experimental data. This study reports 183 C. briggsae mutants belonging to 11 phenotypic classes, which represent the most comprehensive collection to date. Almost all mutants were recovered in EMS screens of the reference strain AF16. Our analysis revealed that 121 mutations define 55 loci and 62 remain unassigned. A combination of complementation tests, linkage tests, two- and three-factor crosses, and polymorphism-based mappings helped place 51 loci and 15 further mutations to the six linkage groups. We report the supporting data, map distances, linkage groups, and corrections to several earlier assignments. Twenty-three loci correspond to molecularly identified orthologs of C. elegans genes, including six for which we report genetic, rescue, or sequence evidence here. The levamisole-resistant mutants fall into at least three complementation groups, two of which correspond to Cbr-unc-38 and Cbr-unc-29 (levamisole-sensitive nicotinic acetylcholine receptor a and non-a subunit, respectively). Transgene rescue experiments identify Cbr-dpy-1 (mucin-like), Cbr-sma-6 (TGFb type receptor kinase), and Cbr-unc-4 (homeodomain transcription factor), genes that have long been in use as genetic markers. In all cases, molecularly identified genes are located on the same chromosome as their C. elegans orthologs, although gene order within chromosomes differs. The strains, map, and underlying data provide a resource for genetic and comparative studies in Caenorhabditis nematodes.

items.title: Evaluating cell-free RNA extraction platforms for RNA liquid biopsy via nanopore sequencing
items.abstract: RNA liquid biopsies provide systemic insights into health and disease by profiling cell-free RNAs (cfRNAs) secreted into the circulation. While cfRNAs are thought to be short or fragmented, recent efforts using long-read nanopore sequencing have found that thousands of longer, full-length cfRNAs are highly abundant in plasma. However, cfRNA extraction methods have not been rigorously evaluated to assess reproducibility, cfRNA length, and transcriptome complexity. Here we show that extraction workflow is a major source of variation by comparing identical plasma samples across three different cfRNA extraction platforms. While these platforms recover comparable quantities of cfRNA, we perform nanopore sequencing to show that they differ in their cfRNA composition based on read-length distribution and biotype representation. Principal component analysis and hierarchical clustering of variable protein-coding and repeat-derived cfRNAs show that samples tend to cluster based on extraction platform. Robust detection of specific biotypes is contingent on extraction platform, as evidenced by significant enrichment of Alu element- and long noncoding RNA (lncRNA)-derived cfRNAs in some but not all methodologies. Our results reveal that cfRNA extraction platforms influence the composition and complexity of downstream libraries, highlighting the importance of selecting the right platform for profiling disease-relevant biomarkers in RNA liquid biopsy studies.

items.title: Replicate libraries set the noise floor for cell-state claims in cross-sectional single-cell data: an empirical audit in drug-tolerant EGFR-mutant PC9 cells
items.corresponding_institution: Scientific Computing Programme, Oswaldo Cruz Foundation (FIOCRUZ), Rio deJaneiro,Brazil.
items.abstract: Claims that drug-tolerant cancer cells occupy stable states rest on single-cell snapshots with one sequencing library per condition, where a difference between conditions cannot be separated from a difference between libraries. No standard says how far a contrast must exceed replicate-library variation. We contribute a replicate-referenced framework: a distance ratio expressing a contrast as a multiple of the distance between replicate libraries of one condition, and a library-level permutation test giving exact p values by relabelling whole libraries. In simulations, single-library tests and a split-half reference rejected a true null in 99 to 100% of runs, and Harmony followed by a cell-level test did so in 12 to 32% with structured library effects. With four libraries per arm, the library-level test held false positives at 3 to 5% in every setting. In public osimertinib-treated PC9 data with two libraries per condition (GSE150949), halves of one library were indistinguishable, replicate libraries separated at 59 to 93% accuracy, and contrasts between times in drug and sort gates exceeded replicate distance 4.5- to 51-fold. In Drop-seq erlotinib data with one library per condition (GSE149383), two libraries of the same condition separated more readily (93.3%) than withdrawn and re-treated cells (88.5%). Cross-sectional contrasts should be reported as multiples of replicate-library distance and, with four or more libraries per arm, tested by library-level permutation. Cells moved away from the untreated profile and stayed away, but the data do not support attractor-style inference, nor do they show that tolerant states are not bistable.

items.title: RR3DD 2.0: an expanded database for RNA three-dimensional structure classification
items.corresponding_institution: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
items.abstract: RNA performs diverse biological functions by folding into specific 3D structures, which are often more conserved than their sequences. Systematic classification of RNA 3D structures is fundamental to understanding structure-function relationships. We previously established RR3DD, the first classification database based on global 3D structural similarity. However, its version 1.0 contained data only up to July 2021 and can no longer reflect the rapidly growing RNA structure space since then. Here, we present RR3DD 2.0. Starting from the 7,466 PDB-format chains in 1.0, we incorporated 8,298 newly released or updated chains, expanding the dataset to 15,764 chains. Pairwise structural similarity (RMscore) was calculated using RMalign, and all chains were re-clustered to yield 1,042 clusters. Compared with 1.0, 2.0 not only increases sampling density but also identifies 342 new clusters. Notably, Cluster-891 and Cluster-899 correspond to the ROOL RNA and GOLLD RNA families, marking the first inclusion of these large structured bacterial ncRNAs into a global classification framework. Mapping the clusters to Rfam annotated 6,388 chains (40.5%) across 154 families. A single cluster can correspond to one or several Rfam families, indicating that global structure classification and sequence family classification are complementary. RR3DD 2.0 provides an updated web interface.

items.title: Period-Specific Remodeling of Luminal Lineages and the Mammary Microenvironment in Dairy Goats
items.abstract: Milk production requires coordinated remodeling of mammary epithelial lineages and their stromal and immune niches, but this process is incompletely resolved in dairy goats. We aim to define period specific cell states and epithelial niche interactions across the dry to lactation transition. We profile mammary tissue from three peak-lactation and three dry-period Saanen goats using 10x Genomics single-cell RNA sequencing and map one peak-lactation goat with Stereo-seq. Among 44,120 cells, we identify15 populations. Peak lactation is characterized by expansion of luminal alveolar cells and increased {beta}-casein and -lactalbumin expression, whereas luminal progenitors, hormone-sensing cells, fibroblasts, and B cells are enriched in the dry period. Trajectory inference place luminal progenitors near branches toward alveolar and hormone-sensing states, with sustained ELF5-associated activity along the alveolar branch. Myoepithelial, macrophage, natural killer T, and T cell states are also remodeled. SPP1 and MIF signaling networks become more connected and change their cellular targets. These data establish a period resolved atlas of dairy goat mammary remodeling and identify coordinated epithelial, stromal, immune, and communication programs associated with active lactation.

items.title: SIREN: Predicting RNA-Small Molecule Interaction using Language Models without Requiring Structure
items.abstract: RNA-targeted drug discovery is constrained by the scarcity of resolved RNA tertiary structures and the conformational flexibility of RNA, which limit the applicability of structure-based virtual screening. Here, SIREN (Small molecule Interaction with RNA via sEquence-based predictioN) is presented, a sequence-based framework that ranks small molecules for a given RNA target directly from its primary sequence without requiring tertiary structure. SIREN integrates a pretrained RNA language model with molecular language model embeddings and physicochemical descriptors through an interaction network that outputs a target-specific compound-ranking score. On four held-out ROBIN riboswitch targets, SIREN outperforms the structure-based methods RNAmigos2, RNAmigos++, and rDock in both enrichment and overall discrimination, and a cross-target derangement analysis confirms that its rankings depend on RNA identity rather than general ligand propensity alone. On an independent HIV-1 TAR benchmark, SIREN achieves strong discrimination without an experimentally derived RNA conformational ensemble. Prospective screening against IRES-derived RNA hairpins from cMyc and XIAP mRNAs further identifies multiple experimentally validated, micromolar-affinity binders from a diverse chemical library. These results demonstrate that SIREN generalizes to unseen RNA targets, transfers across independent benchmarks, and provides a scalable, structure-free framework for RNA-targeted compound prioritization that complements existing structure-based screening approaches.

items.title: Sequence-Derived Geometric Priors Enable Controllable Generation of Intrinsically Disordered Protein Ensembles
items.abstract: Predicting heterogeneous conformational ensembles from sequence remains a central challenge for intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). Sequence-to-ensemble models often entangle geometric inference with coordinate generation, obscuring error sources and limiting control over ensemble properties. Here we introduce MANTA, a C-level framework that separates these stages. An encoder derives geometric priors from protein language-model representations, and a graph-Laplacian decoder converts these priors into conformational ensembles. On a homology-held-out test set, replacing predicted priors with reference-derived priors under the same decoder reduces the median absolute relative radius-of-gyration error from 8.78% to 1.89%, identifying geometric-prior estimation as the dominant bottleneck in MANTA. Across an external benchmark of 27 IDPs, MANTA generates broad, locally valid ensembles. Decoder controls modulate mean compactness and conformational breadth along partially separable axes, while compactness modulation alters motif exposure in tau and amyloid-{beta}. Meanwhile, -synuclein variants shift local exposure populations at nearly unchanged global size. MANTA provides a diagnostic and controllable framework for ensemble generation that captures both global dimensions and local conformational organization.

items.title: Gene regulatory networks and the organization of cell differentiation in multicellular organisms
items.corresponding_institution: Universidad Autonoma de San Luis Potosi
items.abstract: Across their development, clonal multicellular organisms generate new cell types from less differentiated cell types. Differentiation pathways arrange into a hierarchical, tree-like organization: regressions from specialized to undifferentiated cell types rarely occur and undifferentiated cell types often have the potential to produce, when subject to distinct stimuli, two or more differently specialized cell types. How cell type transitions acquire such a peculiar disposition requires an explanation that must reside in the properties of gene regulatory networks (GRNs); after all, GRNs orchestrate the changes in gene activity that define cell types. We studied vast numbers of small dynamic model networks to search for elementary GRNs that could yield the simplest hierarchical, developmental-like, differentiation patterns. We found that only a small minority of GRNs are compatible with hierarchical cell type transitions. Importantly, GRNs that yielded developmental-like differentiation patterns shared common traits: One is the presence of tangles of cycles of positive interactions. Genes in such a tangle produce an all-or-none one-way response to a signal. Another such trait is mutual inhibition between genes associated to different specialized cell types, enforcing their mutually exclusive activation. Moreover, these regulatory patterns are more abundant in published experimentally sustained developmental GRNs than as expected by chance. In addition, we show that it is easy to maintain hierarchical cellular differentiation throughout evolution, even when undergoing changes in gene regulatory interactions and developmental mechanisms. Our work supports the prevalence of design principles that organize hierarchically differentiation pathways in clonal multicellular organisms.

items.title: Neural competition predicts speech production advantages in congenital amusia
items.corresponding_institution: Medical Psychological Center, The Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University
items.abstract: Mental health research has traditionally been deficit-focused, and cognitive advantages in mental conditions have almost always been documented retrospectively. Here we propose and test an a priori pathway for predicting such advantages from a condition's impaired neural basis, neural competition and brain-mind associations. Using congenital amusia (CA), a neurodevelopmental disorder with a well-defined deficit in right frontotemporal circuit (FTC), as a model, we predicted that interhemispheric competition would release the left homologue from inhibition, conferring advantages in speech production. Two independent studies, multimodal neuroimaging and behavioral testing, confirmed this prediction: MRI revealed right FTC impairment alongside competitive-like benefits of the left FTC in CA; and CA showed speech production advantages with intact episodic memory and constrained music learning. These findings provide the first empirical demonstration that cognitive advantages can be predicted in advance and then verified, offering a principled, mechanism-based alternative to the deficit-focused paradigm.

items.title: Resident liver macrophages buffer dietary and circulating cholesterol to maintain hepatocyte homeostasis
items.abstract: Cholesterol metabolism is viewed largely through the lens of hepatocytes, leaving the roles of other liver cells unclear. Using high-resolution live imaging and cholesterol tracing in intact zebrafish, complemented by genetic and clodronate-mediated macrophage depletion and single-cell analysis, we identify liver-resident macrophages (LMs) as cellular buffers of circulating and dietary cholesterol. LMs directly take up cholesterol, and their depletion redirects cholesterol to hepatocytes, which suppress cholesterol synthesis, increase bile-acid synthesis and efflux, and activate metabolic-stress and immune programs, including hepatokine lect2 induction. These responses are heightened by elevated dietary cholesterol and occur without overt inflammation or altered liver architecture. LMs partition cholesterol through abca1b-dependent export and cetp-mediated lipoprotein remodeling. Loss of abca1b causes cholesterol sequestration in LMs and reduced cholesterol-processing demand on hepatocytes, while LM depletion eliminates macrophage-derived cetp and reduces hepatocyte cetp. Together, these findings reveal the innate immune system as integral to normal metabolic physiology, with LMs buffering cholesterol to maintain hepatocyte homeostasis.

items.title: Caenorhabditis elegans HLH-30/TFEB has age-dependent effects on the transcriptome and is required for normal progeny number and larval survival under basal growth conditions
items.abstract: Background: The transcription factor TFEB/HLH-30 is a well-established regulator of autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis during starvation and stress, and it plays important roles in development and homeostasis. Our previous work demonstrated that Caenorhabditis elegans HLH-30 also functions under basal physiological conditions in mature neurons, where it promotes the expansion of endo-lysosomal degradative capacity during early adulthood. These findings raised the question of whether HLH-30 promotes lysosomal gene expression more broadly during early adulthood, and, more generally, whether its basal transcriptional functions depend on animal age. To address these questions, we analyzed the impact of hlh-30 loss on the transcriptome at two larval stages, L1 and L4, and two adult ages, Day 3 and Day 6, in hermaphrodites grown under basal conditions. Results: We identified modest effects of hlh-30 loss on the transcriptome that varied by stage/age. Enrichment analyses of genes downregulated in hlh-30 mutants identified functions related to defense response at L1 and in adulthood, and to cuticle development in adulthood. On the other hand, a role for hlh-30 in the basal expression of autophagy genes was exclusively detected in L1 larvae. A subset of genes encoding cathepsins showed decreased expression in the adult hlh-30 mutant; however, our results indicate that HLH-30 is not broadly required for basal expression of most lysosome biogenesis genes in adulthood. We also detected a trend toward reduced expression of genes involved in germline function at the L4 stage, when spermatogenesis occurs, and found that loss of hlh-30 resulted in reduced sperm and progeny numbers. In addition, we found that hlh-30 is required for full progeny survival through larval development. Finally, we identified a gene with increased expression at all four stages in the hlh-30 mutant, the germline transcription factor-encoding ztf-28. Knockdown of ztf-28 partially suppressed the reductions in progeny number and survival, suggesting that its increased expression contributes to these phenotypes. Conclusions: This study reveals roles for HLH-30 in transcriptome regulation under basal growth conditions that vary in both magnitude and content by animal age. Further, it demonstrates a previously unappreciated requirement for HLH-30 in promoting progeny number and survival, broadening our understanding of the physiological roles of this conserved transcription factor.

items.title: Mapping Senescence Landscapes in Metabolic Liver Disease Progression
items.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects more than 30% of the population, often progressing from reversible steatosis to irreversible fibrosis and cirrhosis. Although cellular senescence is implicated in driving MASLD, the evidence in human tissue and the mechanism are lacking. Here, we apply spatial transcriptomics and scRNAseq to human liver samples spanning healthy to fibrotic disease to address these knowledge gaps. Using a combination of cell stress, cell cycle arrest, extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, and inflammatory genes, senescent microenvironments termed "SenSpots" were identified by Visium transcriptomics that predominantly localized to portal tracts and fibrotic septa across all specimens. Functional profiling revealed a fundamental phenotypic divergence: SenSpots in healthy liver displayed a physiological wound-healing and tissue-development program, whereas SenSpots in fibrotic tissue expressed genes related to inflammation, stress, and ECM-disassembly. Spatial deconvolution and network expansion analyses demonstrated that SenSpots act as epicenters for TGF-{beta}, NOTCH, complement, and ECM-reorganization signaling, which spreads into the surrounding tissue microenvironment as disease advances. Furthermore, scRNAseq data validated the Visium results and identified a previously unappreciated population of senescent Schwann cells in the diseased liver niche. These findings map the spatial origination and paracrine propagation of pathological senescence and identify senotypes associated with liver fibrosis.

items.title: Integrative Multi-Ancestry and Multi-Tissue Fine-Mapping Prioritizes Candidate Causal Genes for Risk of Breast Cancer and Its Subtypes
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Population and Quantitative Health Sciences, Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine, Cleveland, OH, USA
items.abstract: Most breast cancer (BC) risk loci identified by genome wide association studies lie in noncoding regions, and traditional transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) often prioritize multiple correlated genes per locus. We applied two gene fine-mapping methods, TGVIS and M cTWAS, which jointly model gene expression, splicing and alternative polyadenylation (APA) with direct variant effects, to overall BC, estrogen receptor-negative (ER negative) BC and triple-negative BC (TNBC) in women of European and African ancestry. Using 11 BC-relevant GTEx v10 tissues, we prioritized 31, 13 and 5 candidate causal genes, respectively, in European-ancestry populations. Compared with marginal TWAS, fine-mapping reduced the number of candidate genes per locus by 72 to 88%, and credible sets explained 97 to 100% of significant marginal associations. Seven candidates were not reported by previous GTEx v8-based TWAS, including RIN3, supported only by APA, and NPAT for TNBC. Analyses across 48 tissues and brain cell types revealed brain contributions, including ARHGEF5 in oligodendrocytes. In African-ancestry populations, EN1 was prioritized for ER negative BC and TNBC through variants common in African but rare in European ancestry. These results refine BC susceptibility genes, highlight regulatory mechanisms beyond breast tissue and gene expression, and reveal the challenge of mapping GWAS variants to causal genes with currently available data.

items.title: Imaging and Motor Asymmetry in Parkinson's Disease associated with GBA and LRRK2 mutations: Data from the PPMI study
items.corresponding_institution: 1st Department of Neurology, Eginition Hospital, Medical School, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Athens, Greece
items.abstract: Background: According to the -Synuclein Origin site and Connectome (SOC) model, idiopathic Parkinson's Disease (iPD) is classified into two distinct subtypes: symmetric body-first, with diffuse spread and early non-motor clinical manifestations, and asymmetric brain-first, with initially circumscribed motor manifestations. Evidence regarding the application of this model to genetic PD remains limited. Objective: To investigate imaging and motor asymmetry in genetic vs iPD and idiopathic REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (iRBD), addressing thus indirectly the SOC model in genetic PD. Methods: We analyzed demographic, imaging and clinical data from 85 GBA PD, 166 LRRK2 PD, and 912 iPD patients, as well as 30 iRBD participants with abnormal DATSCAN from the PPMI database. Imaging asymmetry was assessed both by Asymmetry Index and absolute Asymmetry difference. Motor asymmetry was calculated as the absolute difference between the MDS-UPDRS III scores of the right and left sides. Results: GBA- and LRRK2-PD patients exhibit more symmetric putaminal radioligand uptake than iPD patients, but greater imaging asymmetry than iRBD subjects in the caudate. iRBD is more symmetric than iPD in both caudate and putamen. Consistent with the imaging data, GBA- and LRRK2-PD exhibit greater clinical motor symmetry than iPD. Conclusion: GBA- and LRRK2-PD are more symmetric than iPD on imaging and clinical grounds. GBA-PD appears to be a predominantly symmetric diffuse synucleinopathy, as predicted by the SOC model. The SOC model may not be applicable to LRRK2-PD, with its predominantly circumscribed motor phenotype, possibly because in this case -Synuclein pathology does not determine lateralization of motor manifestations.

items.title: TP53 and Co-Occurring Pathogenic Variants Are Differentially Associated with Prognosis of Advanced Ovarian and Endometrial Carcinomas
items.corresponding_institution: Internal Medicine Residency Program, Kaiser Permanente, Santa Clara, CA 94051, USA
items.abstract: Objective. To determine whether TP53 and other pathogenic variants (PVs) carry shared or organ-specific prognostic associations in advanced ovarian and endometrial carcinoma. Methods. We analyzed 1060 patients with stage III-IV ovarian carcinoma (924 high-grade serous [HGSOC], 66 clear cell [CCOC], 42 endometrioid, 28 mucinous) and 543 with endometrial carcinoma (EC) profiled by next-generation sequencing. Associations with overall survival (OS) were estimated by multivariable Cox regression and combined across organs by fixed-effect pooling. Key findings were tested in 8881 tumors from public cBioPortal cohorts, including The Cancer Genome Atlas. Results. TP53 PV was associated with worse OS in EC (HR 1.61, 95% CI 1.23-2.10) and CCOC (HR 3.23, 1.05-9.89) but not in HGSOC overall (HR 0.95, 0.72-1.25); in HGSOC, it was associated with worse OS only in KRAS-mutant tumors (HR 3.42, 1.13-10.33). KRAS PV was associated with better OS in CCOC (HR 0.29, 0.09-0.89) and HGSOC (HR 0.72, 0.50-1.02) but not in EC. In HGSOC, BRCA1/2 PV was associated with better OS and MYC amplification with worse OS. In EC, CTNNB1 and ARID1A PVs were associated with better OS. RB1 PV was associated with worse OS in both organs (pooled HR 1.47, 1.05-2.06). In public cohorts stratified by histology, TP53 alteration was associated with worse OS in EC (HR 1.69, 1.36-2.10) and ovarian carcinoma (HR 1.28, 1.00-1.62). Conclusions. The prognostic association of TP53 PV depends on organ, histotype and co-occurring KRAS PV, and RB1 PV is a shared adverse marker. These findings may inform prognostic stratification of Mullerian carcinomas.

items.title: Multimodal population-scale cell atlases define archetypes and extremes of human blood
items.corresponding_institution: Wellcome Sanger Institute, Wellcome Genome Campus, Hinxton, UK
items.abstract: The cellular composition of blood is fundamental to human physiology and is routinely measured to assess health and disease. Circulating immune cells show extensive heterogeneity, but the organising principles and extremes of variation across individuals remain undefined. Here, using single-cell transcriptomics across two biobank cohorts encompassing ~6,000 individuals, we show that human blood occupies recurrent archetypal states defined by coordinated cell composition patterns. We delineate three major archetypes spanning naive lymphoid, myeloid and cytotoxic composition, and two minor archetypes characterised by type I interferon-driven inflammation and expanded premalignant CD5+ B cells. We develop cell2clone to infer lymphocyte clonal expansions, revealing how reactive clonal processes drive the cytotoxic archetype and premalignant clonal expansion establishes the CD5+ B cell archetype, creating outlier states that uncover context-specific effects of germline variants. Clonal haematopoiesis and mosaic chromosomal alterations influence blood states in an archetype-dependent manner. The archetype framework links blood states to common disease risk and clinical blood counts and, through a machine-learning model ArcheTypist, classifies infection and cancer immunotherapy outcomes. This population-scale framework has implications for diagnostics, early disease detection, immunotherapy stratification and mechanistic insights into disease susceptibility and therapy response, providing an organising model for identifying compositional subtypes across human tissues.

items.title: MRCAT: A multi-agent framework for reliable Mendelian randomization analysis and causal interpretation
items.abstract: Mendelian randomization (MR) uses genetic variants to estimate causal effects of exposures on health outcomes, but rigorous MR analyses require coordinated procedures and interpretation under explicit methodological assumptions. Although artificial intelligence (AI) agents can automate analyses, computational completion does not guarantee scientific reliability. Here, we present MRCAT, a multi-agent framework that translates MR-specific knowledge into an AI-assisted workflow that is plannable, executable, verifiable, recoverable and traceable. MRCAT combines dependency-aware planning, Skill-guided execution and expert-informed review with traceable reporting guided by STROBE-MR, a guideline for clear and transparent reporting of MR studies, and iterative Writer-Judge checking. We evaluated MRCAT on 30 natural-language queries spanning diverse data sources, analytical requirements and boundary conditions. MRCAT achieved scientific completion, defined as meeting all nine prespecified MR-specific procedural requirements, for all 26 executable queries and appropriately handled all four boundary cases, compared with 17, 11 and 4 scientifically completed queries for Claude Code, Biomni and BioMedAgent, respectively. Across six independently curated tasks for which the expert-curated analyses did not support causal effects, MRCAT showed closer numerical concordance with the expert-curated analyses and produced interpretations consistent with expert-curated conclusions in all six cases, compared with two for Claude Code and four for Biomni. Additional case studies demonstrated evidence-grounded reporting and selective reuse of analytical outputs in multi-exposure and bidirectional MR investigations. MRCAT provides a framework for reducing the operational burden of MR research while supporting reproducible analysis, assumption-consistent interpretation and traceable scientific reporting.

items.title: Distinct Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging-Derived White Matter Microstructural Phenotypes Tracking Alzheimer's Disease Pathology and Cognitive Decline
items.abstract: White matter (WM) pathology is increasingly recognized as an early, mechanistically relevant feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet sensitive in-vivo biomarkers remain limited. Here, we introduce an MRI-based Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging (RKI) technique sensitive to WM microstructure. RKI metrics differentiate two distinct phenotypes of white matter that follow divergent microstructural trajectories in preclinical and early symptomatic AD. We examined their relationships to AD progression, gray matter (GM) pathology, and clinical impairment in 305 adults spanning amyloid-negative to amyloid-positive stages with normal cognition, preclinical AD, and early symptomatic AD. Pathological changes in one phenotype reflected axonal alterations without myelin loss and were anatomically coupled to GM cortical pathology, strengthening with disease stage - a signature of Wallerian degeneration. Alterations in the other phenotype represented WM demyelination. A model incorporating RKI-metrics, age, sex, amyloid status, APOE genotype, and brain volume classified Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR)-based impairment with an area under the receiver operating curve (AUC) = 0.933, with the RKI-metrics contributing 27% (second only to amyloid at 40%). While both phenotypes related comparably to concurrent cognition (each ~27%), the "axonal" phenotype showed the strongest relationship to subsequent cognitive decline (41% of explained variance), with the "myelin" phenotype contributing 31%. These RKI-defined dual white matter phenotypes provide new insight into AD pathology, adding diagnostic and prognostic value for tracking both current cognitive status and future cognitive decline.

items.title: Vitamin D Insufficiency and Respiratory Muscle Dysfunction in Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1 - A Prospective Cohort Study
items.corresponding_institution: Sahlgrenska Academy, University of Gothenburg, Sahlgrenska University Hopsital
items.abstract: Introduction: Respiratory complications are a leading cause mortality in myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), making it essential to identify modifiable factors that influence long-term pulmonary function. Vitamin D is known to have an important role in muscle physiology, but its potential relevance for respiratory muscle function has previously not been examined in this patient population. Methods: This was a prospective cohort study including patients with genetically verified DM1 (n = 127) aged 18 years or more. Mean follow-up was 4.3 years. All patients underwent a series of examinations including blood tests and measurement of Vitamin D levels and Forced vital capacity % of predicted (FVC%). Results: Vitamin D insufficiency (<50 nmol/L) was present in 43% of participants. Mean FVC% decreased modestly from 65.7% to 63.6% during follow-up (p=0.004). Patients with vitamin D insufficiency had significantly lower FVC% at follow-up compared to those with sufficient levels (54.7% vs 71.2%, p<0.001), and a higher proportion had worsened FVC% (72% vs 50%, p=0.04). In multivariable regression analyses adjusted for disease severity, lower vitamin D levels were independently associated with worse FVC% at follow-up ({beta}=0.12, p=0.04). When vitamin D was examined as a categorical variable in an adjusted model, patients with insufficiency had on average 4.2 percentage points lower FVC% at follow-up compared to those with sufficient levels ({beta}=-4.17, p=0.018), independent of baseline lung function and disease severity. Discussion: Lower baseline Vitamin D levels were strongly related to lung function at follow-up in patients with DM1. These findings remained significant after adjusting for potential confounders. However, because FVC% remained largely stable during follow-up, the possibility to assess the long-term effects of vitamin D on change in respiratory function was limited.

items.title: ProbeFit: one-seizure qualification and personalisation of multimodal wearable seizure detectors
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biomedical Engineering, College of Engineering, Shantou University, Shantou, Guangdong, China
items.abstract: Background and Objective: Missed seizures hinder assessment of seizure frequency and treatment. Although wearables can detect seizures automatically, performance varies between patients. Before deployment, it remains difficult to identify suitable patients, and personalisation usually requires several recorded seizures. We propose ProbeFit to predict later seizure sensitivity and personalise a wearable detector from the first recorded seizure. Methods: We used multicentre SeizeIT2 recordings of behind-the-ear EEG, ECG, EMG and movement from 125 patients. Two generic detectors' peak responses to the first seizure generated a qualification probability. The same seizure and preceding background personalised the detector. ProbeFit was developed on 96 patients and applied unchanged to 29 held-out patients. Expert-labelled video-EEG seizures provided the reference. Evaluation compared qualification with the first-seizure heart-rate rule and measured discrimination, calibration and net benefit, and it compared later sensitivity of the generic and personalised detectors at equal false-alarm rates. Results: Among 27 held-out patients with 152 later seizures, qualification correlated with later sensitivity at Spearman {rho} = 0.38, with one-sided p = 0.033. It identified patients with later sensitivity [≥] 0.5 with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.74. Across all 97 evaluable patients, AUC was 0.76 against 0.59 for the heart-rate rule, a difference of 0.17 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.05 to 0.29. At the qualification threshold of 0.5, ProbeFit withheld deployment from 9 of 15 held-out patients below the sensitivity criterion, and its net benefit was 0.074 against -0.111 for selecting everyone. At equal false-alarm rates between 0.25 and 2 per day, personalisation raised later sensitivity by 2.2 percentage points in held-out patients and by 6.3 points in development patients. Both confidence intervals excluded zero, and no held-out patient lost sensitivity. Conclusions: ProbeFit uses the first recorded seizure to predict whether a wearable detector will detect at least half of a patient's later seizures, and it personalises that detector without waiting for further seizures. It supports patient selection and adaptation during the first monitoring admission.

items.title: A pilot study of the mutational landscape of colorectal cancer in Black South Africans
items.abstract: **Background:** Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a public health concern in sub-Saharan Africa, where the molecular landscape of the disease remains poorly characterised. In particular, genomic studies of resident Black African populations are limited, and the contribution of population-specific mutational processes and potential infectious exposures remains insufficiently understood. The Molecular, Somatic and Infectious Drivers of Colorectal Cancer in Africa (MOSAIC) collaboration aims to address these gaps by generating population-specific genomic data. This pilot study aimed to assess the feasibility of paired tumour-normal whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and to provide an initial characterisation of somatic mutations and mutational signatures in South African patients with CRC. **Methods:** We recruited five Black South African patients with newly diagnosed, treatment-naive CRC through the CoRecT Cancer study at Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital and Wits University Donald Gordon Medical Centre, Johannesburg. Fresh-frozen colorectal tumour tissue and matched peripheral blood samples were subjected to paired-end WGS (2 x 151 bp) using the Illumina NovaSeq X Plus platform. Somatic variants were identified using CaVEMan and Strelka2, followed by functional annotation using the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (VEP). Protein-altering variants were characterised using the R package maftools. Mutational signature contributions were estimated using SigProfilerAssignment and the COSMIC v3 reference catalogue. **Results:** All ten sequencing samples, comprising five tumour-blood pairs, passed quality control. Estimated sequencing depth ranged from 49.2X to 82.4X for tumour samples and from 22.7X to 40.7X for matched blood samples, with a median of 96.3% well-aligned reads. Following somatic variant calling and filtering, the number of retained mutations ranged from 1,106 to 65,379 per tumour. Three of the five tumours harboured at least one predicted protein-altering variant, comprising seven missense and four splice-site variants across eleven genes. Mutational signature analysis of single base substitutions (SBS) revealed inter-individual heterogeneity. SBS1 and SBS5 were detected across all five tumours, while additional signatures included SBS18, SBS20, SBS26 and SBS44, among others. Several tumours exhibited signatures associated with mismatch repair-related mutational processes. **Conclusions:** This pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of paired tumour-normal WGS and preliminary somatic mutation profiling in Black South African patients with CRC. The findings provide initial insights into the heterogeneous mutational landscape of CRC in this underrepresented population. However, the small sample size and incomplete clinical and molecular characterisation necessitate cautious interpretation. Larger studies incorporating comprehensive mismatch repair assessment, copy-number and structural variant analysis, germline susceptibility profiling and investigation of infectious exposures will be essential to validate these preliminary observations and better understand the molecular and environmental drivers of CRC in African populations.

items.title: Additional value of germline genomic scores beyond prostate-specific antigen alone for long-term and near-term prostate cancer risk
items.abstract: We evaluated whether germline genomic risk complements prostate-specific antigen (PSA) for prostate cancer early detection. P-CARE integrates a 601-variant polygenic hazard score, family history, and genetic ancestry. Long-term outcomes and clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) detection on biopsy were assessed in the Million Veteran Program (MVP), with external validation in the Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial (PCPT). Among 428,512 MVP participants, high versus low P-CARE risk was associated with increased hazards of treatment (HR 3.32) and metastasis (HR 3.32). Among men whose baseline PSA was measured at ages 40-49 with PSA 1-3 ng/mL, 15-year treatment/metastasis probabilities were 2.6%, 4.5%, and 10.2% across increasing P-CARE risk groups. High P-CARE risk also predicted csPCa on biopsy (OR 2.96), while PRSPSA was inversely associated with outcomes. Findings were consistent in PCPT. Germline genomic risk complements measured PSA, supporting prospective evaluation of genetically informed screening strategies.

items.title: Hierarchical genetic regulatory architecture of the human immune system informs complex disease mechanisms
items.corresponding_institution: Fondazione Human Technopole, Via Levi Montalcini 1, 20157 Milano, Italy
items.abstract: How inherited genetic variation propagates through multicellular regulatory systems to influence human disease remains poorly understood. To reconstruct the regulatory architecture of genetic variation on circulating immune cells, we analysed single-cell transcriptomes from 6.7 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 4,452 European-ancestry UK Biobank participants, identifying 114,063 independent cis-regulatory effects affecting 15,419 genes. Using a new statistical workflow (FLANDERS), we map the hierarchical organisation of these effects and the underlying regulatory architecture across tissues, immune lineages, cell types and cell states. We find that disease-associated variants predominantly act through regulatory programmes shared within immune lineages and broad cellular compartments, rather than through highly specific cellular states. We show that local cis -regulatory effects commonly act through coherent regulatory pathways implicating transcription factor cascades and intercellular signalling, which allows linking together multiple disease genes. We demonstrate independent support for these genes and mechanisms through rare variant associations. Our findings reveal a highly organised structure of immune regulatory variation shaping human disease, and provide a highly effective framework for interpreting disease associations and prioritising therapeutic targets.

items.title: Circulating immune architecture across age, exposures and disease in ethnically diverse UK cohorts.
items.corresponding_institution: Fondazione Human Technopole, Via Levi Montalcini 1, 20157 Milano, Italy; Wellcome Sanger Institute, Genome Campus, Hinxton, UK; British Heart Foundation Centre
items.abstract: Human immune composition reflects genetic background and cumulative life-course exposures, yet how these influences shape immune architecture across populations and disease remains poorly understood. Here we integrate single-cell transcriptomics, matched clinical haematology and electronic health records from 5,079 individuals of European, British-Pakistani and British-Bangladeshi ancestries to quantify 26 circulating immune cell types and 62 transcriptional states. We map immune compositional variation associated with age, sex, adiposity and smoking, revealing distinct patterns across adulthood and associations between modifiable exposures and advanced immune age. Across common diseases, immune compositional signatures converge on recurrent inflammatory myeloid, adaptive-memory and interferon programmes, whose expression varies with age and population context. Cardiovascular therapies are associated with selective shifts in disease-associated immune states. Immune composition further discriminates common cardiometabolic diseases and resolves patients into endotypes with distinct metabolic and clinical profiles. These findings establish circulating immune architecture as an integrative phenotype linking life-course exposures, population context and disease, providing a framework for precision population immunology.

items.title: Promoter methylation of LDLR is not a common cause of familial hypercholesterolemia
items.corresponding_institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) is a widely prevalent inherited disorder defined by chronically high LDL-C concentrations and a significantly increased risk of cardiovascular disease. While FH is primarily an autosomal dominant disease caused by pathogenic mutations in LDLR, APOB, or PCSK9, approximately 20-60% of clinically diagnosed patients are mutation-negative. A previous survey of over 23,000 methylation profiles identified a differentially methylated region in the promoter of LDLR. This study aimed to investigate whether constitutional hypermethylation of the LDLR promoter is a recurrent cause of FH in patients lacking identifiable pathogenic variants. Methods: We screened 308 mutation-negative clinically confirmed FH patients for promoter hypermethylation in LDLR. We used Combined Bisulfite Restriction Analysis (COBRA) with genomic DNA from peripheral blood samples. The assay assessed methylation at TaqI sites within a 332 bp region of the LDLR promoter. Results: No instances of LDLR promoter hypermethylation were detected among the 308 mutation-negative FH patients. Statistical analysis yielded an upper bound of 1.19% (95% Clopper-Pearson CI) for the prevalence of this specific epimutation in our cohort. Conclusions: Our results indicate that LDLR promoter hypermethylation at this specific locus is not a common cause of the FH phenotype in mutation-negative patients. These findings imply that while methylation in this region may be rare or not significantly contribute to the disease phenotype, the diagnostic gap in FH may be explained by other factors, such as methylation in other regions, polygenic risk, structural variants, or non-canonical regulatory mutations.

items.title: # Treatment- and tissue-context-specific isotope labeling patterns in patient-derived lung cancer tissues: an independent reanalysis of public metabolomics data
items.abstract: Publicly deposited stable-isotope-resolved metabolomics data can be reanalyzed independently, but small patient-derived experiments may produce treatment effects with limited statistical resolution. We reanalyzed a public isotope-resolved metabolomics dataset from patient-derived lung cancer tissue cultures to quantify treatment- and tissue-specific labeling patterns and their uncertainty. We used 38 tissue samples from two patients: matched tumor and non-tumor slices from UK131 treated with vehicle or pembrolizumab and traced with U-13C6-glucose or U-13C5,15N2-glutamine (n = 3 per cell), and a pembrolizumab x WGP {beta}-glucan factorial experiment in UK2035 tumor tissue (n = 3/3/3/2). We recomputed protein-normalized pools, isotopologue distributions, atom-percent excess and pathway summaries. Effects were estimated with log2-scale linear models, Hedges' g, and exact randomization tests that enumerated all assignments compatible with each design; Benjamini-Hochberg q values were calculated within endpoint families. Sixteen macrophage samples were examined only descriptively. In UK131 tumor tissue, labeled non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway intermediates increased 1.84-fold (model P = 0.036; exact tumor P = 0.10; exact interaction P = 0.16; q = 0.32). Weighted isotopic scrambling increased 1.31-fold (exact interaction P = 0.04; q = 0.20), and glutamine-derived glutathione diversion increased 1.66-fold (exact interaction P = 0.09; q = 0.22). In UK2035, the combination increased the labeled IMP/(ATP+GTP+UTP) ratio 3.64-fold (model interaction P = 3.2 x 10-4; exact P = 0.016; q = 0.097). No endpoint survived Benjamini-Hochberg correction at q < 0.05 in the exact analyses. The reanalysis reproduced the direction of the source study's principal labeling patterns but showed that their statistical support is weaker than model-based P values imply. These results should be treated as hypothesis-generating estimates for larger patient-derived studies, not as evidence of a validated metabolic bottleneck.

items.title: Plasma Proteogenomic Uncovers Novel Molecular Mechanisms of Soluble Endoglin and Identifies AZI2 as a new Player in Arteriovenous Malformations in Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia
items.abstract: Endoglin is a transmembrane glycoprotein that plays a key role in vascular development, angiogenesis and endothelial homeostasis. Its soluble form (Sol-ENG), generated through proteolytic shedding of the membrane-bound protein, has been implicated in the pathophysiology of numerous cardiovascular diseases, ranging from common conditions such as preeclampsia and thrombosis to rare diseases such as hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT). Leveraging large-scale genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics data from public and original resources, we identify a molecular signature of 24 markers associated with plasma levels of Sol-ENG. This signature was enriched in genes coding for GPI-enchored proteins and included metabolites participating to glycosylation and redox homeostasis. Furthermore, we observed that ABO blood groups and genetically predicted plasma levels of 5-Azacytidine Induced 2 (AZI2) associate with the risk of arteriovenous malformations in HHT patients. This study provides new insights into the physiological mechanisms underlying Endoglin regulation and opens clinical perspectives for the management of HHT patients.

items.title: A report-supervised EEG-language foundation model enables broad, interactive clinical interpretation
items.corresponding_institution: Section on Computational Neurology, Berlin Institute of Health and Department of Neurology, Charite - Universitatsmedizin Berlin
items.abstract: Medical AI for complex signals such as electroencephalography (EEG) relies on costly expert annotations and predefined diagnostic labels that fail to capture the richness and nuance of clinical interpretation. Whether models trained on routine clinical reports can overcome these limitations while matching expert-supervised performance remains unclear. We introduce EEG Copilot, a biosignal-language foundation model trained on routine EEG-report pairs without dedicated task-specific expert annotations. Across two external datasets (6,078 EEGs), EEG Copilot performed on par with a state-of-the-art expert-supervised model across 11 shared findings (mean AUROC 0.80-0.81), corroborated by direct neurologist review of 200 EEGs. Beyond predefined diagnostic categories in conventional EEG AI, EEG Copilot assessed 23 clinical characteristics through natural-language questions in English and German across 9,689 EEGs from four hospitals (mean AUROC 0.80-0.82), demonstrating that automated EEG assessment need no longer be confined to fixed diagnostic outputs. Crucially, EEG Copilot generated integrated clinical impressions directly from EEG rather than isolated predictions with shuffled-report controls supporting recording-specific content and neurologist review of 800 impressions showing that most were accurate or clinically usable with minor errors. These findings chart a path beyond label-bound medical AI, transforming routine clinical reports into scalable supervision for flexible, language-driven assessment and integrated interpretation of complex physiological signals.

items.title: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis progression is tracked in plasma by systemic proteins independent of motor neurons
items.abstract: Blood biomarkers that change as patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) decline would allow progression to be monitored more objectively. Plasma proteomic studies have identified proteins that differ between patients and controls, but which plasma proteins change as patients decline, and whether they come from motor neurons, is unknown. Here, we leveraged the Answer ALS cohort, with serial SomaScan plasma proteomics, repeated ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised assessments, and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived motor neurons (iMNs) from the same patients. At baseline, 77 plasma proteins differed between 245 patients and 76 controls. These were dominated by muscle proteins, including PDLIM3, ACTN2, and MYOM2, and reflected disease severity. Using a two-stage longitudinal design, we identified 72 progression markers whose within-patient change tracked the rate of functional decline, led by CLEC3B, ANTXR2, and ART3. These were largely distinct from the most elevated muscle proteins and were secreted or shed proteins spread across many tissues. Both sets replicated in the independent Target ALS cohort. A motor neuron expression map built from the iMNs showed that motor neuron proteins were underrepresented in both sets and that expression in iMNs did not predict tracking of decline. Baseline serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) predicted how quickly patients declined but its change did not track decline, whereas change in the progression markers did so within every stratum of baseline NfL. Neither tracked decline in the fastest progressing patients. This positions baseline NfL for prognosis and stratification and systemic plasma proteins for monitoring.

items.title: Exploring the genetic determinants of ALS in a North Indian cohort using a genomic screening approach
items.corresponding_institution: Centre for Genetic Disorders, Institute of Science, Banaras Hindu University
items.abstract: Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a clinically and genetically heterogenous neurodegenerative disorder in which both monogenic and complex genetic mechanism contribute to disease susceptibility. Increasing evidence also indicates that non motor manifestations, including sleep disturbances, significantly influence disease burden. This study aimed to characterize the genetic spectrum of ALS in a predominantly North Indian cohort while evaluating the prevalence of sleep related abnormalities. Methods: Seventy-three clinically diagnosed ALS patients were recruited from a tertiary care centre in North India. Disease severity was assessed using the ALSFRS-R. Sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, and REM sleep behaviour disorder symptoms were evaluated using the PSQI, ESS and RBDQ questionnaires, respectively. Genetic analysis included targeted sequencing of SOD1, TARDBP, and ANG, followed by repeat expansion analysis of C9orf72, ATXN1, ATXN2, ATXN3, and ATXN7. Whole exome sequencing was performed in selected cases to further investigate the genetic basis of ALS. Results: The cohort demonstrated a male predominance and an earlier age of onset compared to many Western populations. Poor sleep quality and excessive daytime sleepiness were frequently observed although no significant association was found between sleep parameters and disease severity. Genetic screening identified a pathogenic/likely pathogenic TARDBP variant classified by ClinVar while no known or novel pathogenic variants were detected in SOD1 or ANG. Repeat expansion studies revealed one patient harbouring pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansions. For the ATXN1, one patient harboured pathogenic repeat expansions and two patients carried intermediate length repeats. Additionally, one patient harboured intermediate repeat expansions in ATXN2. Whole exome sequencing revealed novel and rare variants in ALS associated genes including ANXA11, SIGMAR1, SETX, ERBB4 and NEK1, highlighting substantial genetic heterogeneity. Conclusions: Our findings highlight the complex genetic heterogeneity of ALS, with pathogenic repeat expansions and rare variants identified across multiple disease associated genes. These results demonstrate the importance of comprehensive genetic testing to improve the detection of clinically relevant variants in ALS. In addition, the high prevalence of sleep related disturbances observed in the cohort emphasizes the need to incorporate non motor assessment into routine clinical evaluation of patients with ALS.

items.title: Circulating miRNA profiling identifies hsa-miR-23a-3p and a three-miRNA signature associated with serous ovarian cancer
items.abstract: High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC) is the most lethal subtype of epithelial ovarian cancer, highlighting the need for minimally invasive biomarkers that support disease detection and molecular characterization. Circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) have emerged as promising candidates, although their clinical applicability remains limited by methodological variability and insufficient validation. Plasma samples from 100 individuals (50 patients with ovarian cancer and 50 cancer-free controls) were initially collected from four biobanks. Following quality control, 94 samples (47 patients and 47 controls) were included in the final analysis. Eight candidate miRNAs were quantified using RT-qPCR, and relative expression was assessed following global mean normalization. Differential expression was evaluated using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, while discriminatory performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Three-miRNA logistic regression models were additionally explored using repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation. Among the eight candidates, hsa-miR-23a-3p exhibited significantly lower circulating expression in patients with ovarian cancer than in controls (p = 2.14 x 10^-5), achieving an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.755 (95% CI, 0.657-0.852), with 93.6% sensitivity and 53.2% specificity at the selected threshold. Exploratory analysis across FIGO stages revealed heterogeneous expression patterns, although the limited number of early-stage cases precluded definitive conclusions regarding stage-specific performance. A three-miRNA signature comprising hsa-miR-23a-3p, hsa-miR-21-5p, and hsa-miR-20a-5p achieved an apparent AUC of 0.798. However, repeated cross-validation yielded a mean AUC of 0.716 +/- 0.022, indicating reduced performance after internal validation. Variability in exogenous spike-in Ct values and the marked imbalance in biobank representation between study groups highlighted potential pre-analytical confounding. Circulating hsa-miR-23a-3p showed moderate discriminatory performance between patients with ovarian cancer and cancer-free controls, supporting its further investigation as a candidate liquid biopsy biomarker. Although combining three miRNAs improved apparent classification performance, this advantage was not established through internal validation. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for sample provenance, technical variability, and model overfitting when evaluating circulating miRNA signatures. Independent validation in appropriately balanced cohorts is required before clinical applicability can be established.

items.title: LCatlas: A Point-Of-Care Tool for Predicting Immunotherapy Outcomes in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
items.abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a leading cause of cancer mortality, with a minority of patients experiencing durable responses to first-line immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Currently, there are no easily accessible tools to predict clinical benefit to first-line immunotherapy. To address this gap, we developed LCatlas (https://www.lcatlas.org), a point-of-care web application designed to predict immunotherapy outcomes and inform evidence-based treatment decisions. Using data from 79 NSCLC patients receiving first-line immunotherapy, we extracted demographic, clinical, and molecular features from electronic medical records and compared three independent approaches, statistical model (logistic regression), machine learning (XGboost), and AI model (TabTransformer) to identify the most effective predictor. LCatlas accepts nine variables, gender, smoking history, bone/pleura/liver metastasis, PDL1 tumor staining, albumin level, hemoglobin level, lymphocyte count, neutrophil count, and platelet count, to predict responses to both immunotherapy and immunotherapy plus chemotherapy. LCatlas cross-validation yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 79% [72% - 85%], with sensitivity of 87% [72% - 95%] and specificity of 78% [64% - 89%], outperforming previous studies including high-volume data-driven deep-learning approaches. In a validation cohort consisting of 28 individuals, it demonstrated a prediction accuracy of 82%. LCatlas may serve as a valuable point-of-care tool by identifying patients likely to experience extended immunotherapy or combination therapy using readily available medical data. Its evidence-based approach can optimize personalized treatment planning and thereby promote quality and safety of care.

items.title: Brain Cell-Type-Specific X-Chromosome Gene Regulation Reveals Sex-Biased Candidate Genes in Neurodegeneration
items.abstract: The impact of X-chromosome dosage on gene regulation in specific brain cell-types may importantly shape sex differences in neurodegenerative diseases but remains poorly resolved. We therefore mapped X-chromosome genetic effects on gene expression, i.e. cis-expression quantitative trait loci (cis-eQTL), across seven brain cell-types from 423 old-age individuals. We identified 212 X-linked genes whose expression was genetically regulated, with the majority being cell-type specific. Notably, 10 of these genes (~5%) showed sex-heterogeneous genetic regulation. Through sex-differential expression analyses we further discovered 101 sex-biased genes that were predominantly female-upregulated most strikingly in microglia. Sex-biased gene expression showed both shared and distinct cell-type effects, appearing most divergent in non-neuronal populations. Many female-biased genes overlapped known escape-from-X-inactivation genes and were enriched for links to Alzheimer's disease. Finally, we integrated our resource with X-chromosome-wide association studies of neurodegenerative diseases through causal inference approaches including transcriptome-wide association, mendelian randomization, and colocalization analyses to nominate 11 candidate causal genes, linked to their respective cell-types and sex-informed mechanisms, for Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Multiple System Atrophy. Altogether, our findings suggest escape from X chromosome inactivation may contribute to sex differences in neurodegeneration and provide a resource to advance sex-informed insights into disease pathogenesis and therapeutic opportunities.

items.title: Rare copy number variation in alcohol use disorder using whole-genome sequencing in the All of Us Research Program
items.abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is common, heritable (h2 ~50%) and polygenic, but the contribution of rare structural variation is largely unexamined. Using short-read whole-genome sequencing (srWGS) data from the All of Us Research Program, we tested the association of rare copy number variants (rCNV; minor allele frequency <1%) with AUD in 56,062 participants (5,410 cases, 50,652 controls) defined from electronic health records. Analyses were conducted within European-like (EUR; N=29,392), African-like (AFR; N=8,269) and Admixed American-like (AMR; N=8,049) samples and combined by cross-ancestry meta-analysis. We tested genome-wide rCNV burden, burden within AUD-related, mouse behavioral and neuropsychiatric gene sets, and individual rCNV regions. No genome-wide burden metric or individual rCNV region [≥]10 kb was associated with AUD after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Significant gene-set results were almost exclusively duplications associated with reduced AUD risk across biologically unrelated sets, suggesting a global duplication dosage effect rather than pathway-specific enrichment. In contrast, deletion count within a Neurof_UnionStringent gene set was associated with increased AUD risk (OR=1.04, FDR=0.044), and deletions in xenobiotic-response genes showed nominal associations in multiple ancestry groups. Among rCNV of all sizes, a 58 bp deletion at 16p12.1, a dosage-sensitive neuropsychiatric locus, was significant in the cross-ancestry analysis (OR=2.93, FDR=0.030) without significant heterogeneity. rCNV detectable by srWGS do not appear to contribute substantially to AUD liability at current sample sizes.

items.title: Plasma neurodegeneration biomarkers and clinical progression in early sporadic Parkinson's disease
items.corresponding_institution: Institute for Neurodegenerative Disorders; New Haven, CT, USA
items.abstract: Objectives: Plasma neurodegeneration biomarkers offer an opportunity to characterize Parkinson's disease (PD) biology. The objective of this study was to investigate such biomarkers in deeply-phenotyped participants in Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI). Methods: Baseline plasma samples from early (<2 years since diagnosis) sporadic PD participants with a positive CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (aSyn-SAA) and healthy controls (HC) with a negative aSyn-SAA test were utilized. Plasma P-tau217 (Roche Diagnostics), neurofilament light chain (NfL, Quanterix), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP, Quanterix), and (PD only) amyloid-beta (A{beta}) levels (40 and 42, C2N Diagnostics) were measured. Clinical features at baseline and over up to 11 years were compared across biomarker tertiles in models controlling for age, sex, and baseline outcome variable. Results: The cohort was 97 HC and 523 PD and participants.
