Median [IQR] biomarker values (pg/mL) for HC and PD were P-tau217: 0.14 [0.06 -0.75], 0.15 [0.06 -0.90]; NfL: 10.6 [3.13 -49.85], 12.26 [3.77-62.67]; GFAP: 66.56 [19.75 -403.48], 87.19 [14.55 -531.82]; and in PD A{beta}40: 391.32 [209.95 -538.38]; A{beta}42: 42.74[27.75 -68.55]. No biomarkers differed between HC and PD. In PD, biomarkers were associated with age. In PD only, higher baseline levels of P-tau217 and NfL were associated with greater hazards of a worse cognitive and balance outcome. P-tau217, NfL, and GFAP levels were associated with change in cognitive score over time. Interpretation: Plasma P-tau217, NfL and GFAP levels in early, sporadic PD with confirmed synucleinopathy predict future cognitive and functional impairment, and these findings can inform clinical research design and clinical care.

items.title: Functional and structural neuroplasticity of motor system in hemiplegic cerebral palsy
items.abstract: Hemiplegic cerebral palsy results from a unilateral prenatal or perinatal brain injury and causes motor impairments in the contralateral side of the body. Variable functional outcomes among children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy despite similar lesion extent suggest that developmental neuroplasticity and brain reorganization contribute to motor function. By using multimodal neuroimaging, we characterize the structural and functional reorganization of the motor system and examine its associations with lesion characteristics and upper-limb performance. We examined 26 children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy and 26 typically developing controls using electromagnetic source imaging to map the primary motor cortex and characterize movement-related oscillations across physiologically relevant frequency bands, navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation to assess motor cortical excitability and lateralization, and functionally guided diffusion-weighted MRI to evaluate the structural integrity of descending motor and motor commissural fibers. We further assessed upper-limb function using Melbourne Assessment 2 and examined multimodal relationships using correlation, cross-validated latent-variable, and mediation analyses. Children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy showed microstructural abnormalities in the descending motor and motor commissural fibers, characterized by lower fractional anisotropy and higher mean, axial, and radial diffusivity (all P < 0.05). The navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation identified ipsilateral corticospinal projections from the less affected hemisphere in 17 of 22 children (77%) with hemiplegic cerebral palsy, accompanied by reduced contralesional primary motor cortex lateralization (P < 0.05). The hemiplegic cerebral palsy group also exhibited hemisphere-specific abnormalities in movement-related oscillations, including reduced theta synchronization in the contralesional hemisphere and attenuated mu- and beta-band desynchronization in the ipsilesional hemisphere (all P < 0.05). Larger lesions were associated with poorer motor performance (Rho = -0.74 to -0.57, P < 0.05). Reduced descending motor fiber integrity was associated with impaired dexterity and attenuated mu- and beta-band desynchronization (Rho = -0.51 to 0.62, P < 0.05), while motor commissural fiber integrity was associated with corticospinal motor lateralization (Rho = -0.45 to 0.41, P < 0.05). A cross-validated multimodal structural-functional model predicted motor function (Q^2 = 0.42, P < 0.001) more accurately than structural measures alone (Q^2 = 0.25). Beta-band desynchronization mediated the association between descending motor fiber integrity and motor performance (indirect effect = 0.12 SD, 95% CI 0.03-0.24). Developmental motor neuroplasticity in hemiplegic cerebral palsy reflects an integrated structure-physiology-behavior process rather than the direct consequence of lesion burden alone. Multimodal biomarkers may improve prognostication and support individualized rehabilitation and neuromodulation.

items.title: Microstructure predicts cognition following deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease
items.abstract: Deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (STN-DBS) effectively treats motor and non-motor symptoms in advanced Parkinson's disease (PD). However, 15-20 % of patients experience postoperative cognitive decline and identifying preoperative markers remains an unmet clinical need. In this prospective open-label study, we employed NODDI-DTI to investigate whether cerebral microstructure predicts cognitive outcomes following STN-DBS. Forty PD patients underwent diffusion MRI and neuropsychological assessments at preoperative baseline and 6-month follow-up. A whole-brain voxel-wise analysis related microstructural metrics to postoperative cognitive change. Compromised microstructure within three large-scale networks - the frontoparietal/attentional, default mode/limbic, and ventral associative/visual networks - was associated with greater postoperative cognitive decline. These findings suggest that both disease-related network degeneration and stimulation acting on compromised circuits may contribute to postoperative cognitive decline. In conclusion, preoperative evaluation of microstructural integrity may help identify patients at risk for postoperative cognitive decline, supporting individualised counselling and targeted behavioural monitoring after STN-DBS.

items.title: Carotid Artery Stenosis is Associated with Restless Legs Syndrome in the Absence of Stroke
items.abstract: Background: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a common neurological disorder with established links to atherosclerotic disease and secondary causes such as ischemic stroke. Hypothesizing that internal carotid artery stenosis (CAS) could induce secondary RLS through chronic hypoperfusion or microemboli to dopaminergic subcortical structures, even without overt stroke, we investigated the association between bilateral CAS and RLS. Methods: A retrospective propensity score-matched case-control study was conducted using the TriNetX Global Health Research Network. Cases (n=58,382) had bilateral CAS/occlusion (ICD-10-CM I65.23); controls (n=58,382) had atherosclerosis without CAS. Patients were excluded for prior stroke/TIA, iron deficiency, antipsychotic use, and other secondary RLS causes. Cases and controls were 1:1 matched on age, race/ethnicity, chronic kidney disease, peripheral neuropathy, peripheral artery disease, Parkinson's disease, and SSRI use. The outcome was RLS diagnosis (G25.81), assessed via conditional logistic regression. Results: RLS was diagnosed in 1,154 (1.977%) patients with bilateral CAS/occlusion versus 1,060 (1.816%) controls, yielding an absolute risk difference of 0.161% (95% CI 0.005-0.317%; p=0.0437). The adjusted odds ratio was 1.09 (95% CI 1.002-1.186), indicating a modest but significant association. Conclusion: Severe bilateral CAS/occlusion is associated with a small but statistically significant increase in RLS risk, independently of overt cerebrovascular events and known confounders. These findings support a potential vascular contribution to RLS pathogenesis, possibly through subclinical hypoperfusion affecting basal ganglia dopaminergic pathways. Prospective studies are needed to explore causality, dose-dependency, and the impact of carotid revascularization.

items.title: Evaluation of Semaphorin 3G (SEMA3G) as a biofluid biomarker of cerebral amyloid angiopathy: evidence from neurodegenerative disease and memory clinic cohorts
items.corresponding_institution: Healthy Brain Ageing Program, Brain and Mind Centre, School of Psychology, Faculty of Science, The University of Sydney, Camperdown, NSW, 2050, Australia; Charl
items.abstract: Introduction: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is characterised by amyloid-beta (A{beta}) deposition in cerebral vessels, and frequently co-occurs with Alzheimer's disease (AD). Diagnosis based on MRI-based Boston criteria is not definitive, and CAA biofluid biomarkers are needed. Semaphorin 3G (SEMA3G) was recently shown to be selectively enriched in CAA-affected vessels, and correlated with CAA severity. We therefore evaluated SEMA3G as a biofluid biomarker of CAA. Methods: SEMA3G profiles were examined across diagnoses in the Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium dataset (GNPC) in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (N=1982) and plasma (N=6917). SEMA3G was then evaluated in the Healthy Brain Ageing (HBA) memory clinic cohort (N=161) with 3T MRI, where lobar cerebral microbleed burden was used as a proxy for CAA likelihood, with participants grouped by microbleed count (0, 1-2, or [≥]3). Results: CSF and plasma SEMA3G were significantly lower in AD and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) compared to cognitively unimpaired controls in GNPC, and were associated with hypertension. Longitudinally, plasma SEMA3G declined significantly over time in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and AD. In the HBA cohort, plasma SEMA3G did not differ by cerebral microbleed burden on MRI, nor correlate with plasma A{beta} isoforms and white matter hyperintensities. Discussion: Although CSF and plasma SEMA3G levels were significantly lower in AD and FTD, plasma SEMA3G was not associated with CAA-associated MRI features in individuals at risk of AD. While these findings do not support plasma SEMA3G for identifying individuals with higher CAA-associated burden, its potential utility warrants further evaluation in genetically susceptible or neuropathologically confirmed CAA cohorts.

items.title: CIRCULATING IMMUNE DYNAMICS DURING NEOADJUVANT CHEMOIMMUNOTHERAPY IN EARLY TRIPLE-NEGATIVE BREAST CANCER
items.corresponding_institution: Medical Oncology Department, Hospital Universitario Virgen de la Victoria, 29010, Malaga, Spain; Instituto de Investigacion Biomedica de Malaga y Plataforma en
items.abstract: Background: Pathological complete response (pCR) after pembrolizumab-based neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy predicts improved outcomes in early triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), but circulating immune determinants of response remain poorly characterized. Methods: The study included 64 patients with early TNBC treated with pembrolizumab-based neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy. Flow cytometry analyzed 125 peripheral-blood specimens collected at baseline, during treatment and before surgery. Baseline PBMCs from 22 patients underwent scRNA-seq, generating 135,271 quality-controlled cells. Analyses used nonparametric tests, effect sizes, FDR correction and sensitivity analyses. Results: Baseline scRNA-seq identified response-associated transcriptional differences. Patient-level pseudo-bulk analysis revealed enrichment of TNF-alpha/NF-kappaB signaling in cytotoxic T/NK and B cells from non-pCR patients (global q<=3.94e-7), together with MYC targets and mTORC1 signaling in cytotoxic T/NK cells (both global q=7.00e-5). T-cell analyses suggested preserved naive/memory features in pCR, while a higher proportion of CX3CR1-expressing cells within the CD4 memory/activation-like compartment was associated with pCR (q=0.0157; AUC=0.949). In B cells, pCR was associated with a nominally higher naive-like program score (P=0.029; q=0.059), supported by higher IGHM and IGHD signals, whereas XBP1 was higher in non-pCR. Flow cytometry identified treatment-associated B-cell remodeling. At pre-surgery, switched-memory B-cell CD38 balance was higher in pCR than non-pCR patients (62.6% versus 50.0%; P=0.0086; q=0.0667; Cliff's delta=0.651; AUC=0.825) and remained nominally significant in leave-one-patient-out analyses. Early increases in unswitched-memory B-cell CD38 balance were numerically greater in non-pCR patients, whereas pre-surgery switched-memory B-cell CD38 balance was higher in pCR patients. Conclusions: Baseline inflammatory and metabolic pathway enrichment was associated with non-pCR, whereas pCR-associated T-cell findings included a CD4 memory/activation-associated CX3CR1 signal and trends towards preserved naive/memory features. Together with time- and compartment-dependent B-cell remodeling, these findings nominate circulating transcriptional states and CD38-defined B-cell dynamics for prospective validation as candidate biomarkers of pathological response.

items.title: One blood methylation profile stratifies ten-year risk across 21 common diseases
items.abstract: Blood DNA methylation offers a dynamic readout of inherited and acquired influences on health, creating an opportunity for risk prediction beyond polygenic scores, which are fixed at conception and have yet to demonstrate broad clinical utility. As such, we aimed to develop methylation risk scores for 21 common diseases in 12,785 adults from Generation Scotland and the Mass General Brigham Biobank, combining technically reproducible probes, null-calibrated feature selection and ten-year survival models, with evaluation in a single holdout that was not used for feature selection, model fitting or tuning. The methylation risk scores for eight diseases reached a holdout C-index of at least 0.80: chronic kidney disease, peripheral vascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart failure and type 2 diabetes with at least 50 events each, and interstitial lung disease, dementia and fatty liver disease with fewer. For the five scores with at least 50 events, adjusted hazard ratios per standard deviation ranged from 2.6 to 4.1, with the highest risk tertile containing 73 to 90% of the ten-year events. Panel CpGs were enriched for cytokine signalling, innate immune sensing and sterol metabolism. Against reported values, the eight top-tier methylation risk scores exceed published polygenic and methylation scores alone, and exceed published polygenic and methylation scores that include clinical covariates for seven of the eight diseases (the exception is type 2 diabetes, where our AUC of 0.865 without clinical risk factors is close to a methylation-plus-risk-factor model at 0.872, and our C-index of 0.809 is lower than the C-index for a polygenic-plus-risk-factor at 0.85). These results indicate that a single blood methylation profile can rank ten-year risk for several common diseases at a level that compares favourably with published genetic and methylation scores.

items.title: Circulating gelsolin tracks disease stage in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis across four cohorts
items.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a fatal neurodegenerative disease with highly variable survival, and blood biomarkers beyond neurofilament light chain (NfL) are needed for prognosis and trial stratification. A biomarker of progress through an individualised disease course may be prognostic but independent of the rate of neurodegeneration. We analysed the serum proteome (5,401 proteins) and plasma and cerebrospinal fluid metabolomes (1,659 metabolites) of 94 patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and 39 controls recruited in Sheffield, UK, and replicated findings in cohorts from Tel Aviv, Oxford and the United States (AnswerALS). We defined "disease stage" as the fraction of the onset-to-death interval elapsed at sampling. In contrast we define the rate of neurodegeneration by total survival time or the rate of symptom progression quantified using the D50 model of functional decline. Survival-associated proteins were enriched for stage associations in Sheffield (odds ratio = 5.1) and in the Oxford (2.9), and Tel Aviv (1.6) replication cohorts. Sixty-eight proteins not including NfL tracked stage across four cohorts, implicating systemic inflammation and muscle remodelling; the same biology is tracked by 149 plasma and 58 CSF stage-associated metabolites. Stage-associated proteins that rose with stage also rose with age in UK Biobank (17 of 17 age-associated proteins), and the proteomic age gap rose nominally with disease stage (partial Spearman r = 0.25, P = 0.027; BH-adjusted P = 0.055). Circulating gelsolin (GSN) fell with advancing disease in all four cohorts. NfL tracked disease aggressiveness (beta = 0.56, P < 0.001) but not stage (0.13, P = 0.056), whereas GSN tracked stage (-0.41, P <0.001) but not the rate of symptom progression (-0.08, P = 0.25). GSN explained 10% of the variance between patients in disease stage quantified by survival time and 19% of the variance in stage quantified by functional decline; this is comparable to the variance in the rate of neurodegeneration which is captured by circulating NfL. Accounting for disease stage separates markers of disease rate from markers of disease position, refining both biomarker discovery and biological interpretation in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
